We present a novel method for quantifying the molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies by utilizing the subthermally excited C I 113 $\mu$m and 158 $\mu$m lines. This approach relies on the fact that the C I 113 $\mu$m line is the strongest among the low-excitation carbon monoxide transitions, making it an ideal tracer for low-density gas. We demonstrate that the C I 113 $\mu$m line luminosity correlates with the molecular gas reservoir mass of galaxies, a relationship that remains consistent regardless of metallicity. Furthermore, this line exhibits a strong correlation with the CO(2-1) line luminosity, which is the conventional standard for estimating molecular gas reservoirs. Consequently, C I 113 $\mu$m serves as a viable alternative to CO(2-1) for measuring molecular gas reservoirs, particularly in the far-infrared bands accessible to the Herschel Space Observatory.

This paper introduces a novel code-switching treebank constructed from Frisian-Dutch data, incorporating 1,000 sentences from the Frisian-Dutch Switchboard corpus. To achieve accurate annotation of morphological and syntactic properties, the authors employed a hybrid approach combining a pre-trained language model with human oversight. We also developed a specialized lexicon to map both languages onto a unified UD tree structure. Furthermore, the paper analyzes the code-switching patterns present in the dataset.

This study investigates the impact of stellar mass on the photoevaporation of protoplanetary discs, utilizing a suite of 100 hydrodynamical simulations. These models cover a stellar mass range of 0.1 to 0.4 solar masses and an initial disc mass range of 0.01 to 0.1 solar masses, with disc ages spanning from 1 Myr to 10 Myr. The simulations employ a new, self-consistent model for disc photoevaporation that incorporates the effects of FUV, X-ray, and EUV radiation. The results indicate that more massive stars possess higher FUV and X-ray luminosities, leading to more rapid disc dispersal. Consequently, the disc mass distribution shifts toward lower masses for higher stellar masses, and the disc mass function (DMMF) evolves toward a shallower slope. Furthermore, the disc mass function's slope steepens with time, and the timescale for disc dispersal increases with greater initial disc mass. The study also examines the relationship between disc mass and stellar age, revealing that the disc mass function for a specific star mass is best described by a power law with a slope of -1.35. The findings suggest that disc photoevaporation is a primary driver of disc mass evolution, with the most significant effects occurring in systems hosting more massive stars.

This study introduces a novel category of explicit generalized-$\alpha$ schemes designed for isogeometric analysis of structural dynamics. These methods are characterized by their ability to handle highly stiff systems effectively, offering arbitrarily high order accuracy without imposing a Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) constraint. By utilizing the Isogeometric Analysis (IGA) framework, the approach leverages the superior convergence rates of the method to reduce the number of degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. Furthermore, the proposed methods maintain the advantageous low numerical dissipation of traditional generalized-$\alpha$ techniques. A key contribution is the derivation of explicit formulas for the required numerical parameters, which are shown to depend solely on the polynomial degree of the IGA basis functions. Consequently, these parameters remain constant across all elements within a single mesh, regardless of variations in element size.

This study investigates the dynamics of a Bose polaron within a one-dimensional double-well, specifically focusing on the decay of the polaronic residue. We demonstrate that the polaron's stability is governed by the competition between the energy required to create intra- and interband excitations. Furthermore, we derive analytical expressions for the decay rates associated with both excitation types, which are essential for determining the polaron's lifetime.

This study examines a multi-stage stochastic programming framework designed for the optimal allocation of emergency supplies. The methodology employs a two-phase approach: first, a deterministic model is established to represent the anticipated average scenario, followed by the integration of stochastic elements to address uncertainty regarding the timing, location, and scale of disasters. The resulting stochastic model is solved using a scenario tree-based technique. The methodology is applied to a case study involving the strategic distribution of relief items across multiple potential disaster sites. The analysis evaluates the trade-offs between computational efficiency and solution quality by comparing results from a static deterministic model against various dynamic stochastic models with different numbers of stages. The findings indicate that a three-stage dynamic model offers the most effective balance between these factors. The study concludes with a discussion on the practical implications of these results.

Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are expected to detect gravitational waves (GWs) generated by compact binary inspirals within the Galactic Center. While the signal from such binaries is theoretically most pronounced when the GW source maintains a high orbital eccentricity, the resulting GW-induced timing residuals in pulsars are also strongly modulated by this eccentricity. This study presents a novel, fully analytical framework for calculating pulsar timing signals from inspiralling eccentric binaries, achieving accuracy up to the 2.5 post-Newtonian (2.5PN) order. Our methodology relies on a perturbative approach that expands the timing residuals as a power series in orbital eccentricity, with each term derived using time-domain waveforms accurate to the 2.5PN order. We have validated the precision of our analytical expressions by comparing them against numerical results, and we have also assessed the computational efficiency of our method relative to existing approaches.

This study examines how individuals react to shared signals regarding the average level of action within a group. We present a framework where participants face uncertainty about both private costs and the average action, reacting to global signals that provide information about the former. We establish conditions ensuring that best responses remain unique and demonstrate that responses are generally sensitive to the prior distribution of average actions, except in specific cases. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of signal precision and identify scenarios where herding occurs. By calibrating our global game to a social coordination experiment, we find that the model accurately predicts the data.

This study introduces a technique for characterizing high-loss dielectric liquids within the 750 GHz to 1100 GHz frequency range. The method utilizes a coplanar waveguide (CPW) with a suspended dielectric sample, employing a vector network analyzer to measure the resulting changes in the waveguide's S-parameters. By applying a closed-form analytical model, the dielectric constant and loss tangent of the liquid are derived directly from these S-parameter measurements. The viability of this approach is demonstrated through the evaluation of two high-loss substances: a 10% (w/v) glycerol solution and a 10% (w/v) sucrose solution.

The AIRSENSE-TO-ACT initiative, a European project, aims to develop a comprehensive, multi-layered, and data-driven framework for managing the pandemic. This framework integrates diverse data sources, including meteorological conditions, air quality metrics, and clinical records, to address the challenges of the current crisis. The project's primary objective is to create a robust, multi-source data processing system capable of analyzing these varied inputs to generate actionable insights. This analytical output will inform the creation of a decision support tool designed to guide the implementation of effective countermeasures, thereby assisting policymakers in managing the evolving pandemic landscape.

This paper introduces a smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) framework designed for multi-resolution simulations of multi-phase fluid-structure interactions. The approach employs a hybrid method combining a grid-based solver for the bulk of the flow with SPH particles localized near free surfaces and interfaces with solid boundaries. The grid solver utilizes a high-order finite-difference scheme for convection and a compact finite-difference scheme for diffusion, whereas the SPH component relies on a newly developed multi-resolution kernel function. The multi-phase interaction is modeled using a volume-of-fluid (VOF) technique. The study examines the kernel function's performance across various particle distributions and spacing ratios, alongside the impact of artificial viscosity on the interface between phases. The proposed method's efficacy is validated through simulations involving two-phase flows around a moving cylinder and a breaking dam-broken scenario.

Nodal lines within momentum space represent one-dimensional, topologically protected crossings between energy bands. These structures are characterized by non-trivial topological invariants, which mandate the presence of Berry phase singularities within the surrounding two-dimensional plane. Such line nodes have been observed in various contexts, including photonic systems, cold atoms, and condensed matter physics. This study offers a comprehensive review of these topological attributes and their associated physical phenomena. Furthermore, we detail a cold atom experimental platform capable of engineering and detecting these line nodes. We also analyze the topological invariants for T-joints connecting these line nodes and demonstrate how they can be verified experimentally. Finally, we present a method to manipulate the topological charge of these line nodes using cold atoms.

This document outlines the needs for event generators within the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) era. It examines the challenges of simulating high-momentum particles and the specific computational and storage resources required to address them. The text further analyzes the feasibility of meeting these demands through hardware acceleration and explores alternative solutions, such as utilizing modern accelerator computing. Finally, the review offers recommendations concerning software development strategies and organizational structures aimed at fulfilling these requirements.

This article establishes a property characterizing the support of a probability measure through its partial means. As a consequence, it is demonstrated that the support can be reconstructed as the closure of the set generated by the union of the hyperplanes representing the measure's partial means.

We present a novel detection of a thick disk of molecular gas in the outer galaxy, identified through the analysis of the CO(1-0) line emission from the outer Milky Way. This finding is derived from a comprehensive survey of the CO(1-0) line across the entire northern hemisphere, conducted using the Nobeyama Radio Observatory (NRO) 45-meter telescope. The study reveals that the molecular gas distribution in the outer galaxy is characterized by a two-component structure: a thin disk and a thick disk. The thin disk, which dominates the inner galaxy, exhibits a scale height of approximately 300 pc, whereas the thick disk, prevalent in the outer galaxy, has a significantly larger scale height of about 1.5 kpc. Furthermore, the molecular gas fraction in the outer galaxy is roughly 10 times greater than in the inner galaxy, suggesting that the formation of the thick disk is linked to the low surface density of the gas. The detection of the thick disk in the outer galaxy is significant because it implies that the outer galaxy contains a substantial reservoir of molecular gas, which could play a crucial role in the formation of the supermassive black hole residing in the galactic center.

This study examines a closed economy where a government seeks to maximize social welfare by adjusting taxes and public spending. The analysis utilizes the Kykloz model, which employs a log-linearized New Keynesian DSGE framework. The paper outlines the optimal strategies for both the government and the private sector, alongside the resulting equilibrium outcomes.

This study investigates collective dynamics in disordered polar active matter, specifically examining how interactions between particle alignment and motility influence behavior. We observe that when active motility drives particles apart, the system undergoes a transition from disordered to ordered states as motility decreases, a process driven by alignment interactions. Conversely, strong repulsive motility maintains disorder. We identify a critical threshold of motility below which the system exhibits large-scale collective motion, a phenomenon that is notably more pronounced in conditions of low motility.

This study investigates the semileptonic decays of doubly charmed baryons, specifically $\Xi_{cc}^+$, $\Omega_{cc}^+$, and $\Xi_{c}^{++}$, utilizing the bag model. The decay form factors are determined by matching the matrix elements derived from the weak effective Hamiltonian with those calculated within the bag model framework. Results indicate that the semileptonic decay rates for these baryons are suppressed by a factor of approximately $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-5}$ relative to singly charmed baryon decays. Consequently, the corresponding branching fractions fall within the range of $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-3}$.

This study introduces a novel approach to localization within embodied systems by leveraging dialogue. While dialogues can reveal the presence of objects and individuals, they are also capable of conveying spatial details, such as the exact positions of entities. Our method utilizes these conversational insights to estimate the user's location. Our primary contributions are twofold: first, we develop a dataset comprising 1,000 synthetic conversations, each annotated with ground-truth entity locations, to train our model. Second, we present a novel architecture that integrates a recurrent neural network with a neural process to map conversational data directly to location estimates. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves performance on par with state-of-the-art localization techniques.

This paper introduces a new methodology for automatically selecting frequency bands in vibration analysis, designed to enhance the detection of machine faults. The approach is founded on the Band Relevance Factor (BRF), a metric that quantifies the importance of specific frequency bands. The BRF integrates two key parameters: the energy contained within a band and the statistical dispersion of that energy. By combining these elements, the method identifies frequency bands that exhibit high energy levels with significant variation across different machine states. The BRF's effectiveness is demonstrated through two case studies: the first involves selecting frequency bands for a gearbox using simulated data, and the second involves selecting bands for a bearing using real-world data.

Muon-spin relaxation and rotation studies were conducted on the noncentrosymmetric superconductors CaIrSi$_3$ and CaPtSi$_3$ to investigate their superconducting ground states. In CaIrSi$_3$, the muon-spin relaxation rate ($\lambda$) increases with temperature, indicating a single superconducting gap. Conversely, in CaPtSi$_3$, $\lambda$ exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on temperature, suggesting the presence of two superconducting gaps. Furthermore, the gap anisotropy in CaIrSi$_3$ is significantly lower than that of CaPtSi$_3$. These findings align with the expected properties of noncentrosymmetric superconductors, where spin-orbit coupling strength is critical in shaping the superconducting ground state.

This study introduces a novel approach to solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation for stochastic optimal control problems, leveraging a sparse grid characteristic technique. This method effectively mitigates the curse of dimensionality inherent in high-dimensional stochastic control. We establish the theoretical foundation of this approach by demonstrating its equivalence to a collocation scheme utilizing multivariate orthogonal polynomials. Furthermore, we prove the convergence of this collocation method and derive error bounds for the numerical solution of the HJB equation. We also present an algorithm to numerically solve the HJB equation, alongside an analysis of the resulting optimal feedback control law. Finally, we validate the proposed method through various numerical examples, highlighting its superior performance compared to conventional finite difference methods.

We present a classification of quantum measurements based on the equivalence of their Kraus operators' singular values. This classification aligns with the freedom to change measurement Kraus bases under invertible transformations, a property that remains invariant under stochastic equivalence of quantum channels. We demonstrate that these newly defined equivalence classes correspond to a generalized framework for quantum entanglement. Furthermore, we explore connections with existing literature and propose a protocol for distinguishing quantum measurements through local operations and classical communication.

This study introduces a novel framework for analyzing and managing multi-energy dynamical systems, which are fundamental to the decarbonization of modern infrastructure. We formulate these systems using a differential algebraic equation (DAE) approach, where the algebraic components are defined by nonlinear, non-smooth, non-convex constraints. We establish that, under specific conditions, the resulting optimization problems are equivalent to a specific class of DAEs. Furthermore, we present a new algorithm designed to solve these governing equations, demonstrating its efficacy through applications in both static and dynamic scenarios.

We investigate the two-dimensional percolation model on a square lattice, utilizing machine learning techniques to extract universal properties from a vast ensemble of configurations. By analyzing the distribution of cluster sizes, we derive the cluster size exponent, which aligns with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, examining the distribution of the number of clusters yields the scaling function and fractal dimension of the percolating cluster; these results show excellent agreement with prior theoretical and numerical studies.

This study introduces a rapid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) approach for tracking temperature dynamics within gas-solid fixed beds. The method utilizes a $^{12}C$ NMR technique combined with a $^{12}C$ probe, leveraging the temperature-dependent chemical shift of $^{12}C$ nuclei to generate real-time, three-dimensional thermal maps. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach can acquire temperature maps of the entire fixed bed at 1 mm spatial resolution and 10 seconds temporal resolution. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential of this method for analyzing thermal phenomena in complex, heterogeneous systems.

We introduce a phenomenological framework for superconductivity featuring quenched disorder and thermal fluctuations, which generates a reentrant superconducting phase situated between the normal state and the primary superconducting phase. This theoretical model is applicable to unconventional superconductors characterized by a multi-component order parameter. Specifically, we examine uranium cobalt-dodide (UTe$_2$), a candidate for intrinsic magnetic-field-induced topological superconductivity. Our analysis reveals that quenched disorder and fluctuation-driven reentrance are compatible with experimental findings, including the observed reentrant signature in zero-field specific heat and the suppression of the superconducting critical temperature under magnetic fields.

Ultra-wideband (UWB) technology is a short-range, low-power communication standard capable of precisely estimating distances between devices. It achieves this by transmitting radio signals across a wide spectrum of 3.1 to 10.3 GHz, allowing receivers to select the optimal physical layer (PHY) configuration for the current environment. However, the performance of these radio settings fluctuates as the surrounding environment changes. This paper introduces a novel deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach to automatically adjust PHY parameters in real-time. The method employs a DRL agent to learn the optimal set of radio settings for a specific scenario, subsequently using this agent to manage PHY configuration on a UWB device. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly surpasses traditional manual tuning methods.

This paper investigates the k-median clustering problem within the context of geometric string and path sets, utilizing both the discrete Fréchet and Hausdorff distance metrics. We demonstrate that the k-median clustering problem is NP-hard for both distance measures. Furthermore, we establish an approximation algorithm with a constant factor of 4 for the discrete Fréchet distance, which relies on a dynamic programming approach with exponential complexity relative to the number of clusters. Finally, we prove that the k-median clustering problem is also NP-hard when applied to Hausdorff distance.

Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has emerged as a promising approach for addressing complex, large-scale optimization problems. However, current MARL methods face significant hurdles, including non-convergence, high computational costs, and a lack of theoretical guarantees. To address these issues, we introduce a MARL framework that integrates the Q-learning algorithm with an optimization perspective. Specifically, we model MARL as a constrained, monotropic variational inequality (VI) problem and solve it using a double-averaging primal-dual algorithm. This approach offers several advantages: it is straightforward to implement, supports parallel computation, and provides provable convergence to a solution set. Furthermore, numerical experiments on the classic "Hawk-Dove" game demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques in terms of both speed and accuracy.

This paper introduces a general framework for satisfiability checking within coalgebraic $\mu$-calculi, specifically designed to accommodate various fixed-point logics and transition systems. The framework demonstrates its utility across three distinct logics: the well-established first-order $\mu$-calculus, the arithmetic $\mu$-calculus, and the arithmetic fragment of the $\mu$-calculus. The proposed satisfiability algorithm is proven to be complete and operates with an exponential space complexity relative to the input formula's size.

This study introduces a new approach for recovering sparse initial states in isogeometric analysis (IGA) problems. The method leverages the low-rank structure of a specific Green's function, which is derived from the kernel of the integral operator linked to the Isogeometric forward map. This kernel is constructed using a low-rank approximation of the low-rank structure of a specific Green's function, derived from the kernel of the integral operator linked to the forward map. The method is validated through numerical experiments on a one-dimensional heat equation and a two-dimensional wave equation, both solved using IGA. These tests demonstrate the method's ability to successfully recover sparse initial states in problems involving low-rank structures of a specific Green's function, derived from the kernel of the integral operator linked to the forward map. This study introduces a drive-by sensing approach for generating dense maps of air quality. The proposed method utilizes a facility location algorithm to identify optimal driving routes for data collection, subsequently deploying a deep learning model to forecast pollutant levels at stationary points based on this route information. The system's efficacy is demonstrated through the creation of high-resolution air quality maps for the Los Angeles metropolitan area. The resulting predictions are contrasted with those derived from a dense network of fixed air quality monitors. The deep learning model's performance is rigorously evaluated using a dataset comprising drive-by observations from Los Angeles, New York, and the greater London area. The results indicate that the drive-by predictions are comparable in accuracy to those from fixed monitors, with the drive-by approach offering the distinct advantage of greater flexibility in data collection.

This paper establishes the Weil representation for the ring of truncated polynomials over a finite field, specifically for the general linear group, under conditions of a second-class involution. Furthermore, it examines the irreducibility of this representation and the corresponding branching laws.

Persuasive digital media, such as social networking posts, advertisements, and political content, is designed to influence human behavior by fostering positive attitudes and driving actions. The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has spurred the creation of AI-driven persuasive media generation systems capable of customizing content for specific audiences. This survey offers a comprehensive overview of current research regarding AI-enabled persuasive video generation. We begin by defining core concepts and categorizing various persuasion techniques. Subsequently, we examine AI-driven video generation methods, outlining their applications in creating persuasive content. Finally, we highlight emerging trends and potential future research avenues.

We introduce a unified theoretical framework for the quantum behavior of ions in quadrupole and octupole ion traps, accounting for the squeezed coherent states of motion (SCSMS) that emerge from the combined effects of ion-ion and ion-axial interactions. This approach allows for the derivation of SCSMS for the fundamental ion mode, which are characterized by a specific squeezing parameter and center. Furthermore, we calculate the SCSMS for higher-order ion modes and evaluate their corresponding squeezing parameters and centers. This comprehensive method enables the precise calculation of ion mode wave functions, facilitating the derivation of key physical properties such as ion mode frequencies, ground state temperatures, and ion-ion interaction strengths.

Neuroscience models are increasingly intricate, making it difficult to identify the most suitable parameters for specific tasks. Consequently, there is a growing need for automated frameworks capable of efficiently navigating these hyper-parameter landscapes. In this work, we introduce a novel framework designed to explore such spaces by leveraging meta-knowledge from previously solved problems. We demonstrate that this approach can significantly boost the efficiency of hyper-parameter exploration in neuroscience models. Specifically, we apply this method to a neural network tasked with classifying the direction of motion in biological motion images. Experimental results indicate that our framework achieves superior performance compared to conventional methods.

Camouflaged objects are defined by their blending into the background, making them difficult to distinguish. While numerous studies have focused on detecting and segmenting these objects, a significant gap remains in the lack of a standardized benchmark for evaluating instance segmentation performance in wild environments. To address this, we introduce the Camouflaged Instance Segmentation Benchmark Suite (CIS-BSuite), a comprehensive tool designed to assess the performance of various methods. This suite comprises a curated collection of 10 publicly available datasets, along with a novel evaluation metric that accounts for both detection and segmentation accuracy. We apply the suite to test twelve state-of-the-art approaches, including those adapted from single-object detection and camouflage classification. Our findings reveal that current methods achieve only moderate results, highlighting the urgent need for future research in this domain. Additionally, we present CIS-BSuite, a new method that leverages the unique challenges of wild camouflage to deliver superior performance. Experiments demonstrate that CIS-BSuite surpasses all competitors on every dataset, with its source code and models available at https://github.com/zhengshenghuang/CIS-BSuite.

We examine the effects of Lorentz violation on superconductivity, specifically focusing on the Ginzburg-Landau framework. Our analysis reveals that Lorentz violation induces a $T$-odd component in the superconducting order parameter, which generates a $T$-odd contribution to the supercurrent. This effect is driven by the $T$-odd part of the order parameter, which is a $p$-wave component. We also investigate the impact of this Lorentz-violating term on the critical magnetic field and note that its influence on the superconducting state is markedly stronger in type-II materials compared to type-I materials.

As Artificial Intelligence systems are increasingly integrated into critical areas like healthcare and finance, ensuring their safety and reliability has become paramount. However, identifying and mitigating AI errors remains a significant hurdle, particularly when models are deployed in production environments. This paper introduces a novel methodology for detecting and validating these errors by leveraging crowdsourced failure reports. We present a dataset of such reports, which were verified by a domain expert, and demonstrate that this approach enables the identification of diverse error types, including hallucinations, biases, and factual inaccuracies.

Object detection has seen significant advancements in recent years, yet it remains computationally intensive, making it unsuitable for real-time applications. To address this, we introduce R(Det)^2, a randomization-based routing method designed to enhance detection efficiency. Our approach involves a randomization step that selectively assigns bounding boxes to different detectors, thereby reducing the computational load. We demonstrate that this technique can be integrated with any existing object detection architecture. Furthermore, we show that R(Det)^2 maintains high accuracy comparable to the original method while achieving a substantial reduction in computation. Specifically, we observe up to a 3.5x speedup in detection speed with only a minimal 0.1% drop in mAP.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are highly susceptible to adversarial attacks, which involve creating inputs that are nearly indistinguishable from the original but cause the model to produce incorrect outputs. While Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) is a potent white-box attack capable of generating such adversarial examples with a single step, the corresponding adversisory training approach suffers from catastrophic overfitting. This phenomenon occurs when the model learns to fit adversarial data rather than benign samples, leading to a significant drop in performance on clean inputs. This study introduces ZeroGrad, a novel training method designed to address catastrophic overfitting. ZeroGrad is derived from the ZeroShot Adversarial Training (ZSAT) framework, which utilizes adversarial examples from an out-of-distribution class to mitigate catastrophic overfitting. By substituting the source of adversarial examples with those generated via FGSM, ZeroGrad offers a streamlined and efficient solution. Empirical results demonstrate that ZeroGrad effectively combats catastrophic overfitting, achieving superior robustness compared to existing adversisory training techniques. Furthermore, the study provides an analysis of the mechanisms underlying catastrophic overfitting and offers practical recommendations for practitioners.

This study examines the Thakurta metric, a proposed solution to Einstein's equations for a cosmological black hole, and argues that it fails to meet the necessary conditions for physical viability. Specifically, the Thakurta metric exhibits a singularity at $r=0$ that is not a physical curvature singularity but a coordinate singularity, and it violates the energy conditions required by general relativity. These findings imply that the Thakurta metric cannot serve as a valid description for cosmological black holes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these issues undermine recent claims suggesting that constraints on primordial black hole (PBH) abundance derived from LIGO-Virgo observations of black hole mergers depend on this metric. We conclude that such claims of dependency are unfounded, and the validity of LIGO-Virko bounds on PBHs remains intact regardless of these arguments.

This study examines the impact of persistent asset switching on a specific class of optimization algorithms inspired by hysteresis, which are frequently employed in control theory. We demonstrate that these algorithms exhibit stability under persistent switching conditions when the step sizes are sufficiently small. Furthermore, we establish the rate of convergence for the generated asset values toward a global minimum of the objective function. The analysis relies on the concept of a Lyapunov-like function, representing the discrepancy between current and prior asset choices, as well as the deviation between the current set of prices and those from a previous epoch.

Bootstrapping represents a critical challenge in fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), a field that enables computations on encrypted data without exposing the underlying plaintext. This paper introduces BTS, a novel bootstrapping framework designed to enhance efficiency and lower resource demands. By leveraging a new set of encrypable functions, BTS streamlines the bootstrapping process, achieving a 2.5x reduction in runtime and a 3.5x decrease in memory usage compared to the current state-of-the-art.

This work examines the large-$N$ limit of the $\beta$-ensemble featuring a logarithmic confining potential, $V(x) = \ln |x|$. We demonstrate that the eigenvalue density $\rho(x)$ is supported on the entire real line and decays as $e^{-1/2|x|}$ at infinity. Furthermore, we derive the exact solution for the correlation function $\rho_2(x,y)$, from which all higher-order correlation functions can be determined.

This study experimentally investigates quantum correlations within a two-qutrit spin system using a pair of continuous-wave quantum dots driven by a two-tone radio-frequency (rf) field. The resulting dynamics are modeled using a generalized Bell state, and the system's behavior is analyzed through two key metrics: quantum discord and concurrence. The findings indicate that while both quantum correlations reach their maximum at the same point, their behaviors diverge significantly elsewhere; specifically, the peaks for quantum discord are broader than those for concurrence. Additionally, the data reveals that these quantum correlations are more resilient against decoherence than single-qutrit systems.

This study introduces a quantum model of a bipartite system that exhibits correlations exceeding any classical framework, yet remains free of nonlocality and violates no Bell inequalities. The proposed architecture relies on two spatially separated laboratories, each housing multiple isolated quantum subsystems that interact solely within their respective environments. Although the specific internal dynamics are indistinguishable, the global interactions between the labs generate the strong observed correlations. The only assumption required is that these hidden internal degrees of freedom are inaccessible to the researchers. The paper further demonstrates that such an arrangement permits the derivation of quantum laws governing the visible degrees of freedom from those hidden ones, provided one accepts the principle of local causality. The work concludes by arguing that this conclusion implies factorizability is a natural consequence of locality, rather than requiring the additional assumption of measurement independence.

We introduce StyleGAN-V, a video generation architecture that leverages the StyleGAN2 framework. This model supports the continuous synthesis of videos with arbitrary lengths, including those exceeding 100 seconds, while maintaining high visual fidelity. Our approach achieves this by integrating a temporal component into the generator, which is trained on the complete dataset rather than short video segments. Consequently, StyleGAN-V offers a unified, end-to-end solution for generating both short and extremely long videos without requiring separate models for different durations. Furthermore, the system is designed to be scalable, allowing for efficient training on massive datasets. Our experiments demonstrate that StyleGAN-V produces superior quality outputs compared to existing video generation methods, while also exhibiting enhanced robustness against adversarial attacks.
The text outlines a method for calculating the variation in degrees for pairs of self-dual newforms that are linked via Eta correspondence, applicable when the self-intersection number is non-zero.

Accurately determining the glow curve's peak time is essential for high-quality signal retrieval in dosimetry. Traditionally, this process involves manual analysis of the curve's peak, a method prone to human error. While a machine learning approach utilizing a support vector machine (SVM) has previously been developed to estimate peak times, this study presents a deep learning alternative using a convolutional neural network (CNN). The CNN was trained on a dataset of 1,000 manually annotated glow curves and subsequently evaluated against a test set of 100 curves. The results demonstrated that the CNN significantly outperformed the SVM, achieving a reduction in average estimation error from 1.4% to 0.4%.

This paper examines a category of singular problems involving a distinct double-phase nonhomogeneous variational equation defined on a complete manifold. By employing techniques derived from variational methods, Sobolev-Orlicz spaces, and the truncation method, we establish the existence of solutions for these equations.

The Fastcat simulator, developed by the University of Manchester, offers a high-performance solution for simulating cone beam CT (CBCT) data at both kilovoltage and megavoltage levels. This study evaluates the Fastcat simulator by comparing its kilovoltage outputs against CBCT scans acquired using the Elekta Versa HD platform. The analysis involved three anthropomorphic phantoms: a CIRS CTDI phantom, a Gammex 2030 head phantom, and a Gammex 402 chest phantom. For each scan, a single projection was simulated and directly compared to its corresponding measurement. The Fastcat simulator demonstrated strong agreement with the measured data, yielding a mean relative error of 1.1% across all projections. This level of accuracy confirms that the Fastcat simulator is suitable for applications involving CBCT image reconstruction, dosimetric analysis, and image-guided interventions.

Machine learning models are increasingly ubiquitous across diverse fields, yet their complex internal mechanisms often remain opaque. To address this lack of transparency, numerous interpretability methods have emerged, with LIME (Local Interpretable Model-averaged Explanations) being a prominent example. LIME operates by perturbing input data and training local approximating models to elucidate specific predictions. However, LIME is susceptible to sampling instability, which can result in inconsistent and unreliable explanations. This paper introduces a novel method, S-LIME, designed to mitigate such instability. S-LIME integrates a bootstrap technique with a bootstrap confidence interval to filter out unstable explanations. We evaluate our approach against LIME using both synthetic and real-world datasets. Results demonstrate that S-LIME generates explanations that are not only more consistent but also more accurate than standard LIME.

This study introduces a Bayesian framework designed to correct classification errors by leveraging user feedback on explanations. The approach is grounded in Bayesian decision theory, which guides the selection of the most probable explanation for a given input. The model employs a structured generative approach to construct a probabilistic distribution over explanations, utilizing a neural network to parameterize this distribution. The neural network learns to map inputs and their associated incorrect labels into explanation spaces, with the resulting generative model then correcting errors by sampling explanations and selecting those with the highest probability. The system is trained on a dataset containing explanation labels for a subset of examples and operates by generating explanations for the remainder. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework effectively recovers classification mistakes on the unseen examples.

The study of the spin-liquid candidate TbInO$_3$ using inelastic neutron scattering reveals a spectrum of crystal-field excitations. These excitations are well-modeled by a crystal-field Hamiltonian incorporating a significant anisotropic term, $E_{z}$. The findings indicate that the ground state is a $J_{z} = \pm 15/2$ doublet, while the first excited state is a $J_{z} = \pm 13/2$ doublet situated at 1.15 meV. The second excited state is a $J_{z} = \pm 11/2$ doublet located at 2.15 meV. Furthermore, the data supports the presence of vibronic modes within the crystal-field spectrum. The observed energy splitting between the ground and first excited states is attributed to the anisotropic crystal-field component $E_{z}$, which arises from the triangular lattice's inherent geometric frustration.

We establish that convex power-of-mean curvature flows, defined on convex initial hypersurfaces in Euclidean space, evolve smoothly over time and maintain their convexity throughout the evolution process.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in numerous computer vision tasks, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely obscure. This study investigates the frequency domain characteristics of CNNs and introduces a novel architecture called the Frequency Neural Network (FNet), which executes convolutions directly within the frequency domain. By performing operations in the frequency domain, FNet significantly reduces computational costs and enhances parameter efficiency. Furthermore, we developed a new training methodology designed to optimize the weights of the Fourier transform kernels. Empirical evaluations across various datasets reveal that FNet surpasses CNNs in both accuracy and efficiency, while also shedding light on the frequency domain insights gained about CNN operations.

This study introduces a new image clustering method called DeepCluE, which leverages multi-layer ensembles within deep neural networks. The approach utilizes a deep neural network to extract features from the input data, with clustering performed at multiple layers by integrating the outputs of these layers. To achieve this, we developed a new ensemble technique named "DeepCluE," which combines the outputs of different clustering algorithms applied at various layers. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, where it achieved superior clustering performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

This paper introduces a new framework designed to detect institutional risks by analyzing news articles, utilizing a hybrid approach that combines knowledge graphs with automated news profiling. This system aggregates and structures data from various sources, including public reports, official statements, and regulatory filings, to generate a comprehensive knowledge graph. To identify potential risks, we employ a profiling method that applies scoring algorithms to text from news sources and official statements, comparing them against the institutional data derived from the knowledge graph. This approach enables a holistic assessment of an institution's risk profile by integrating multiple information sources. We validated the method's effectiveness by applying it to a sample of 100 European banks, demonstrating its ability to successfully identify risks.

This study presents a novel approach to classification leveraging Topological Data Analysis (TDA). The method utilizes the persistent homology of a point cloud to detect topological characteristics, such as loops and voids, which are then integrated into a subsequent classification phase. We evaluate this strategy on synthetic datasets and on data from the scikit-learn repository, comparing its performance against standard machine learning techniques. The outcomes indicate that this TDA-based method is particularly effective for distinguishing between clusters with identical dimensions and varying homology.

This paper presents a characterization of contra-simarity through the lens of two-player games. In this framework, one player seeks to construct a contra-similar link between two given representations of potentially differing dimensions, while the other attempts to prevent this. We demonstrate that if both players utilize a deterministic strategy with a finite set of options, a winning strategy is guaranteed for the player attempting to establish the contra-similar relationship.

We provide a construction for a string 2-group representation equipped with a monoidal structure. This serves as the higher-level analog to how the string group represents loop group representations in traditional fashion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any such representation naturally forms a string group cocycle, thereby defining a specific $E_2$-inner automorphism.

The study examines the formation of ion-acoustic solitary waves and rogue waves within a double pair plasma comprising non-extensive electrons and ions alongside equal numbers of antiparticles. Utilizing the reductive perturbation technique, the derived Korteweg-de Vries-Maxwell (KMV) equation describes these ion-acoustic waves. The analysis reveals that the amplitude of the solitary waves is modulated by the ratio of electron to antielectron noise temperature, the plasma's temperature, and the non-extensive parameter. Furthermore, the phase and group velocities depend on the plasma's composition, the non-extensive parameter, and the wave amplitude. Under the reductive perturbation approximation, the Cubic Nonlinear Schrödinger (CNS) equation is derived to describe rogue wave dynamics. The primary characteristics of these rogue waves are governed by the plasma's constituent composition, the non-extensive parameter, and the amplitude modulation factor.

The parametric decay instability (PDI) of Alfvén waves is a primary mechanism for converting magnetic energy into heat and particle acceleration in space plasmas. This study investigates the PDI within a laboratory-relevant plasma by employing a hybrid kinetic-fluid simulation code. In this model, the ion fluid is simulated using a multi-fluid approach, while electrons are represented as a single fluid species, and ion kinetic effects are captured through Landau fluid theory. The simulation demonstrates that the PDI can be triggered in a magnetized plasma by injecting a high-amplitude Alfvén wave. The results indicate that the instability is driven by ion Landau damping, which is facilitated by the finite ion-to-ion mass ratio. Furthermore, the study examines the influence of plasma beta on the PDI, revealing that the instability is suppressed when beta is sufficiently high.

We investigate the gravitational instability of filamentary molecular clouds, accounting for ambipolar diffusion, by analyzing the dispersion relation of longitudinal density perturbations. Our results indicate that the filament's aspect ratio is a critical parameter for determining its stability. Specifically, a high aspect ratio promotes instability, whereas a low aspect ratio favors a stable state. Furthermore, we observe that the critical mass for instability is lower in unstable filaments compared to stable ones. The inclusion of ambipolar diffusion results in a reduced growth rate for unstable filaments and an elevated critical mass threshold. Additionally, we find that ambipolar diffusion exerts a more significant influence on filaments with lower densities.

We investigate the time evolution of a two-level system coupled to a bosonic bath, where the system-bath interaction strength is comparable to the frequency gap between the system's energy levels. By employing a non-perturbative approach, we demonstrate that the system can exhibit both the quantum Zeno and anti-Zeno effects, provided the bath spectral density follows a specific functional form.

This study introduces a distributed trajectory planning approach for quadrotor swarms that ensures collision avoidance. The method relies on a linear safe corridor (LSC) technique, which models the relative motion of each drone with respect to its neighbors using linear constraints. This framework is integrated into a distributed model predictive control (MPC) scheme, enabling each agent to compute trajectories based on real-time neighbor information. To ensure robustness against communication delays and packet loss, the LSC formulation incorporates specific constraints that maintain inter-agent safety despite these disturbances. The proposed algorithm's feasibility and performance are validated through both simulation and physical experiments.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has gained significant traction in computer vision, particularly for lane detection tasks, where the goal is to transfer models trained on simulated data to real-world scenarios. While existing UDA methods typically target a single domain shift, such as from simulators to one specific real-world environment, this paper introduces CARLANE, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates the transfer from various simulators to multiple real-world datasets. CARLANE encompasses four distinct simulators and four real-world datasets, with the latter featuring a novel dataset, "Sim2Real LaneNet," which is the first to include a transfer from a simulator to four different real-world domains. To facilitate UDA research, CARLANE provides a complete dataset containing annotated images, along with comprehensive statistics and baseline performance metrics. Additionally, we release a detailed analysis of the current state of the art in UDA for lane detection, aiming to establish a robust benchmark for future advancements.

The study investigates the influence of a hydrophobic particle layer on the wetting and contact angle behavior of a hydrogel substrate. Results indicate that these hydrophobic particles significantly lower the receding contact angle, with the effect intensifying as particle size increases. This phenomenon is attributed to the ability of larger particles to induce greater substrate deformation, thereby increasing the density of particles exposed at the surface. Furthermore, the reduction in contact angle correlates with the particles' contact area fraction and their contact line pinning effect.

This study examines the correlation between student connectivity and academic performance, utilizing data from a cohort of 1,000 students who completed a semester of online learning during the pandemic. Connectivity was assessed through a digital platform that tracked every interaction, including participation in video classes, discussion board posts, and the submission of assignments. Academic outcomes were measured by final grades and student self-evaluations. The analysis reveals a strong positive correlation between the frequency of student interactions and higher course grades. Furthermore, students who engaged with peers more often also reported greater satisfaction with their learning experience. These findings reinforce the value of active engagement for both individual success and the collective progress of the class.

This study introduces a novel approach for rapidly estimating wind profiles using the combination of the European Space Agency's MetOp-A satellite's Advanced Scatterometer (ASCAT) and the European Meteorological Satellite Organization's Meteosat First Generation (MSG-FG) L-band Doppler radar. The method leverages the MSG-FG's high temporal resolution to capture the swift evolution of wind fields, while the ASCAT data provides high-resolution vertical profiling. To bridge these datasets, an autoregressive model is trained on ASCAT wind measurements to forecast surface wind speeds at one-hour intervals. The MSG-FG Doppler data then serves to correct these forecasts, significantly enhancing their accuracy. The system was tested on a case study involving a tropical cyclone, demonstrating that the MSG-FG data improved ASCAT's forecast precision by 10%. This advancement enables the generation of high-resolution, three-dimensional wind profiles with a vertical resolution of 500 meters and a horizontal resolution of 25 kilometers.

We present a detailed study of UBC 274, a young open cluster in the process of disruption. Utilizing data from the Hubble Space Telescope's Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) and the Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3), we analyzed the cluster's morphology, kinematics, and chemical composition. Our findings reveal that UBC 274 is a young, metal-rich cluster with a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] = +0.17 ± 0.04, situated within the Milky Way's thin disk. The cluster exhibits a distinct elongated structure, with a major axis of 1.2 pc and a minor axis of 0.3 pc. The quality of neural machine translation (NMT) is heavily contingent upon training data. While synthetic trans lation offers a promising method for expanding bitext datasets, its impact on subsequent NMT model performance remains uncertain. This study evaluates whether bitexts enhanced with synthetic translations yield superior results compared to those augmented with high-quality professional translations. We examine this by analyzing bilingual error patterns, applying various text mining strategies, and conducting controlled NMT training experiments. Our findings indicate that although synthetic trans lations can improve bitext quality under specific conditions, professional translations generally produce better outcomes.

We investigate the dynamics of entanglement in quantum spin chains subject to engineered dissipation, specifically focusing on the shift from logarithmic to area-law scaling. By utilizing the matrix product operator formalism, we analyze the time evolution of the von Neumann entropy for bipartite entanglement. Our results indicate that the nature of this entanglement transition is highly sensitive to the dissipation Hamiltonian. Specifically, we demonstrate that while dissipative cooling of the ground state generally yields a two-qubit entanglement area law, this outcome can be reversed by applying a suitable local term to the Hamiltonian governing the dissipative process.

We examine the spin-orbit coupling within transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers, specifically focusing on flat bands. Our analysis indicates that when the atomic layers are stacked in a B-type configuration, the coupling between the layers induces a significant enhancement of the intrinsic single-layer spin-orbit interaction. This process generates a substantial interlayer exchange coupling, which is tunable by adjusting the composition of the constituent monolayers. Conversely, the coupling between the layers in an A-type stacking mode remains minimal, resulting in a markedly weaker exchange coupling.

We introduce a quantum reservoir computing framework designed for digital quantum simulation within finite-dimensional systems. This approach leverages the chaotic dynamics of a finite-dimensional quantum reservoir to function as a universal computational tool capable of approximating any continuous function. We provide a rigorous mathematical proof of function approximation validity grounded in quantum control theory, which outlines the specific conditions required for the system's chaotic behavior. Furthermore, we propose a practical experimental realization using an N-dimensional quantum system driven by a time-varying control Hamiltonian. This implementation is validated through a numerical simulation of a three-level quantum reservoir encoded on a single qutrit, which successfully performs function approximation.

We propose a method for stably trapping neutral atoms using the near-field of a GaN-on-sapphire chip equipped with an integrated planar dipole antenna. This approach offers a favorable balance between high trapping efficiency and minimal perturbation to the atoms, achieved by leveraging the high dielectric constant of gallium nitride alongside the low loss characteristics of low-temperature co-fired ceramic (LTCC) sapphire. We demonstrate that this system can generate robust optical dipole traps, capable of retaining a single Bose-Einstein condensate of ${}^{87}$Rb at microwave frequencies of 5.8 GHz and 11.2 GHz. Furthermore, we show that the trap's high aspect ratio facilitates the creation of a narrow, high-density beam of ${}^{87}$Rb, which serves as an ideal input for subsequent experiments involving atom interferometry and quantum information processing.

This work introduces and evaluates two finite element approaches for solving Poisson's equation: the classic Lagrange element method and a newer mixed formulation. Both techniques are implemented using the open-source library MFEM, which supports various element types, including those of higher orders. The Lagrange method employs standard Gauss quadrature for integration, whereas the mixed formulation utilizes Gauss-Radau quadrature. The mixed approach offers distinct benefits, such as the ability to directly compute fluxes and the avoidance of spurious non-physical pressure modes. However, it is noted that the mixed formulation can be more computationally intensive than the Lagragian counterpart. The study demonstrates that the Gauss-Radau quadrature used in the mixed method is equivalent to employing Gauss-Laguerre quadrature on a shifted polynomial basis within the Lagragian framework. Furthermore, the mixed element method is shown to be more efficient regarding the condition number of the system matrix.

This study examines a specific class of interacting dark energy models characterized by a sign-changing interaction term dependent on the Hubble parameter, specifically $Q = 3H\Lambda_0\exp[-\alpha H]$, where $\Lambda_0$ and $\alpha$ are constants. We analyze the dynamical stability of these models within the framework of Friedmann-Lema\^{\i}tre-Robertson-Walker cosmology, determining the evolution of energy density transfer between dark components and the corresponding scale factor's behavior. Furthermore, we evaluate the evolution of statefinder diagnostics and the equation of state parameter across different epochs. Our findings indicate that the interaction term transitions from positive to negative values, with the interaction strength peaking at early times and subsequently diminishing. We demonstrate that the model's early-time behavior mimics phantom dark energy, whereas late-time evolution aligns with standard dark energy characteristics. Additionally, the analysis suggests that the early universe is dominated by dark radiation, followed by dark matter domination, and that spatial curvature becomes relevant only at late times.

The radio flares observed in tidal disruption events (TDEs) are widely believed to originate from relativistic jets, yet the specific mechanism driving particle acceleration remains uncertain. This study investigates the acceleration of electrons within these jets using the quasi-perpendicular shock acceleration framework. We model the jet as a relativistic shock wave propagating through a stationary ambient medium, assuming the shock normal is nearly perpendicular to the magnetic field. By applying a test-particle approximation to the kinetic equations, we derive the temporal evolution of the electron distribution function. The resulting power-law spectrum is characterized by a spectral index of $\alpha = 1.5$, a cutoff energy of $E_{\rm max} \sim 0.1\gamma_{\rm s}m_ec^2$, and a total energy fraction of $\sim 0.1\gamma_{\rm s}^{-1}$. These findings align well with the spectral indices and cutoff energies observed in radio flares from TDEs, supporting quasi-perpendicular shock acceleration as a viable mechanism for particle energization in these events.

Acoustic cavitation is a phenomenon where the rapid expansion and collapse of microbubbles occurs within an acoustic field, a process that generates significant local temperatures and pressures. This study investigates the resonant behavior of microbubbles in an acoustic field by analyzing the time-domain solution of the Keller-Miksis equation. The analysis focuses on bubbles with a radius of 10 micrometers, driven by a peak pressure of 100 kPa at a frequency of 28.56 kHz. The results indicate that these bubbles reach a maximum radius of 10.5 micrometers and exhibit a peak velocity of 1.2 m/s. Additionally, the study examines the impact of varying the driving frequency on the bubble's time-domain response.

Emotion and stress regulation are vital for human health, with stress often leading to severe conditions like anxiety and depression. While wearable technology has gained popularity for monitoring these states, current methods frequently rely on a single modality, resulting in low detection accuracy. This paper introduces MUSER, a novel framework designed to address stress detection through multimodal data. By utilizing emotion recognition as an auxiliary task, MUSER leverages the strong correlation between emotional states and stress to boost performance. The system comprises a multimodal emotion recognition module and a stress detection module, with the former serving as support for the latter. We evaluated MUSER using the public Multimodal Stress Dataset (MSD), comparing it against state-of-the-art models. Our results demonstrate that MUSER achieves superior accuracy in stress detection compared to these existing benchmarks.

We introduce PanGEA, a toolkit designed for annotating panoramic graphs that capture 3D environmental geometry. This 3D representation encodes the spatial arrangement of points sampled from an environment, enabling downstream tasks such as scene reconstruction, semantic labeling, and scene graph generation. To support this, PanGEA offers a comprehensive suite of tools for importing, visualizing, and annotating panoramic graphs, alongside a collection of diverse environments sourced from various sources. The utility of the toolkit is demonstrated through a case study involving the annotation of a panoramic graph derived from a 3D reconstruction of a museum gallery.

The "downsizing" phenomenon describes the trend where massive elliptical galaxies (EGGs) cease forming stars earlier than lower-mass galaxies. This study examines the downsizing trend through the lens of the IllustrisTNG simulation, specifically analyzing the stellar mass dependence of the star formation timescale ($t_{\rm SF}$) for EGGs. The analysis utilizes a novel, environment-dependent stellar initial mass function (IMF) and a SNIa rate that scales with the EGGs' environment. The results indicate that the IMF and SNIa modeling significantly impact the EGGs' $t_{\rm SF}$ evolution. Specifically, the IMF and SNIa models are found to be crucial for accurately reproducing the observed stellar mass dependence of $t_{\rm SF}$. Furthermore, the study finds that the EGGs' $t_{\rm SF}$ is highly sensitive to the SNIa rate, with variations in the IMF and SNIa models capable of shifting $t_{\rm SF}$ by up to 1.5 Gyr. These findings underscore the necessity of accounting for the IMF and SNIa models when investigating the downsizing phenomenon.

This study introduces a new approach to image compressive sensing reconstruction grounded in group-based sparse representation and non-convex regularization. The proposed method comprises two distinct phases: (1) a dictionary learning stage that identifies group sparsity patterns within an over-complete dictionary tailored to the target image, and (2) a reconstruction stage that utilizes a non-convex group sparsity prior for iterative image recovery. The group sparsity patterns are derived using a novel algorithm based on the $p$-norm ($0 < p < 1$) to promote non-convex group sparsity. Theoretically, this $p$-norm prior is proven to possess a non-empty null space, ensuring the existence of a solution for image recovery. Furthermore, the group sparsity prior is shown to be more effective than the traditional $l_0$-norm at achieving superior sparsity. Experimental results confirm that the proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in both computational efficiency and reconstruction accuracy.

This study introduces a novel approach to identifying facial skin issues by detecting the specific locations of defects on skin rather than analyzing the entire image. We define this technique as "object-by-object learning," a method that enhances the detection of minor defects by focusing exclusively on the affected areas. To achieve this, we developed a new deep learning architecture named RethNet, which utilizes a region-based detection framework. Unlike traditional methods that analyze full images, our approach involves a two-stage process: first, a skin region is segmented from the background, and second, a convolutional neural network analyzes the cropped skin area to identify defects. We evaluated the RethNet model on the FAUST dataset, a comprehensive collection of 1,000 images featuring various skin conditions. Our results demonstrate that RethNet outperforms existing object-detection models in identifying defects on the FAUST benchmark.

This work examines the performance and complexity of parallel access codes (PACs) when using sequential decoding. PACs are a class of random coding schemes that guarantee constant decoding error probabilities in the large blocklength limit, provided the channel is non-degenerate and the decoder is maximum likelihood (ML) or near-ML. Although sequential decoding is widely used for block codes due to its low average computational complexity, its application to random codes has traditionally been limited to cases with infinite average blocklengths. In this study, we demonstrate that for PACs, the average complexity of sequential decoding remains bounded even at finite blocklengths. Furthermore, we derive a lower bound on the error probability of the sequential decoder under a fixed average complexity constraint. These findings are supported by numerical simulations.

Recommendation systems are vital for e-commerce platforms, yet they face significant challenges with cold-start users who possess minimal interaction history. While many existing methods attempt to address cold-start user and item representation learning by leveraging side information, they often fail to fully utilize the sequential nature of user preferences. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Seq2Seq-ML, a sequential recommendation framework for cold-start users that integrates both meta-learning and transitional learning. Specifically, we utilize transitional learning to capture the temporal dependencies within user behavior sequences, while employing meta-learning to transfer knowledge from non-cold-start users to those who are cold-start. Empirical evaluations on two real-world datasets demonstrate that Seq2Seq-ML outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines, achieving substantial improvements in both accuracy and robustness specifically regarding cold-start recommendations.

This overview provides a concise review of the current status of ultra-high energy cosmic rays, covering their experimental observations, measured energy spectra, composition, and arrival directions, as well as the theoretical models attempting to explain these observations.

The DART mission represents the inaugural active planetary defense test, aiming to alter the orbit of the Didymos binary asteroid system by colliding a kinetic impactor with its secondary body, Dimorphos. This study examines how the projectile's shape affects momentum transfer efficiency, analyzing both spherical projectiles and a practical polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) rod. Using the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) method, we modeled the collision dynamics and crater formation. Our findings indicate that while spherical projectiles yield a consistent momentum transfer efficiency of approximately 3.6, the rod-shaped projectile demonstrates a significantly higher efficiency of 5.2. This increase is attributed to the projectile's elongated geometry, which facilitates a deeper penetration into the target. Consequently, these results suggest that the trajectory of the kinetic impactor should be optimized to maximize the transfer of momentum.

Driver identification is a critical component of vehicle safety. To ensure driver presence and correct seating orientation, driver recognition systems are essential. This paper introduces the Mertens Unrolled Network (MU-Net), a deep learning architecture designed to identify drivers through vehicle windshields from a distance. MU-Net integrates two fusion modules: the first combines the Mertens Layer (utilizing a high dynamic range technique) with a standard convolutional neural network, while the second merges a pre-trained face recognition model with another convolutional neural network. Experimental results indicate that MU-Net surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in driver recognition accuracy.

The development of new programming languages is a common occurrence, yet many established ones, such as Python, Perl, and C, boast extensive repositories of mature code. The Comprehensive Blub Archive Network (CBA-N) is a proposed network of open-source repositories dedicated to these newer and older languages. This paper introduces the CBA-N, outlines its design philosophy, and presents initial findings on the network's growth and the nature of languages represented within it.

This paper introduces a new class of semiparametric estimators designed to estimate population means in settings involving missing data for both covariates and outcomes. These estimators are built upon a weighted augmented inverse probability weighting (IPW) score, where the weights are defined as a weighted inverse probability of missingness. The approach is flexible enough to accommodate various missingness mechanisms, including non-monotone, partially missing outcomes, and missing not at random (NMAR) scenarios. The methodology is notably advantageous because it separates the estimation of missing data probabilities from the modeling of the outcome, allowing for the use of simpler models for the outcome when the data generating process is complex. The authors establish the asymptotic normality of the proposed estimators and provide a simulation study demonstrating their robustness under both missing at random (MAR) and missing not at random (NMAR) conditions. The study concludes by applying the method to a real-world dataset from a randomized trial investigating the impact of a behavioral intervention on physical activity levels.

This study examines a conjecture by T. Hasegawa and the second author regarding the approximation of the complete elliptic integral of the first kind using the inverse hyperbolic tangent. Specifically, it proves an inequality that strengthens Hasegaga's original inequality and establishes an optimal (sharp) bound.

This paper addresses the challenge of learning inductive procedures from examples. While recent methods have demonstrated success in this area, they are constrained to a fixed, finite collection of procedures. In contrast, we introduce a novel algorithm capable of discovering an arbitrary procedure, provided the solution space is bounded by a finite number of functions. Our approach decomposes a high-dimensional function learning task into multiple lower-dimensional subproblems, leveraging this structure to achieve superior performance. We demonstrate this advantage through a novel variant of the k-Nearest Neighbor algorithm, which learns continuous functions from high-dimensional inputs to outputs. We provide theoretical assurances for this variant, proving it can learn any continuous function within a compact domain with a finite set of possible outputs. Furthermore, we show that this decomposition strategy yields significant practical speedups for the k-Nearest Neighbor algorithm.

The rise of social media has led to an unprecedented surge in the circulation of fake news, prompting a need for this study to examine how machine-generated content can be identified. Specifically, we investigated the effectiveness of various Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques in identifying fabricated news articles created by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Our analysis focused on Arabic news stories spanning diverse subjects and political contexts, produced using the Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) and the Latent Variable Model (LVM). We evaluated these models against human-written articles and news forgeries created by a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) using a similar Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) approach. Our findings indicate that GAN-generated text is significantly more difficult to distinguish from authentic news than RNN-generated text.
