We introduce a novel approach for reconstructing generic handheld objects in three dimensions. Our method utilizes a combination of a single RGB image and a single RGB-D image, with the depth map being the only input requiring no manual annotation. We achieve this by training a network to generate a 3D point cloud from the depth data, subsequently refining this cloud to align with the visual appearance of the target object. This process is executed in an end-to-end framework, utilizing a large-scale dataset comprising 3D models and images of everyday items. Our experiments demonstrate that our method produces high-quality 3D reconstructions for generic objects, even when the input depth maps are of low resolution.

The Ca-K index serves as a primary indicator of chromospheric activity, reflecting the intensity of plage regions within the solar chromosphere. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of Ca-K index variations derived from a century-long dataset collected at Kodaikanal Observatory, India. By utilizing image equalization techniques, we generated a dataset spanning 1917 to 2017, which was subsequently analyzed using a novel method to determine plage area coverage. This approach involves calculating the mean and standard deviation of pixel values across the entire disk, followed by identifying plage regions where pixel values fall below the mean minus one standard deviation. This methodological innovation allows for the direct estimation of plage area coverage. Our results indicate that plage area coverage exhibits a strong correlation with chromospheric activity, peaking during solar maximum and declining during solar minimum. Furthermore, we observed a significant link between plage area coverage and sunspot numbers, with a correlation coefficient of 0.85. This study underscores the utility of the Ca-K index as a reliable proxy for monitoring solar activity over extended periods.

This study reports the first observation of the rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, with a measured branching fraction of $(7.1 \pm 0.9 \pm 0.7) \times 10^{-8}$. The first uncertainty is statistical, while the second is systematic. The measurement utilizes a data sample of $1.0 \text{ fb}^{-1}$ of $pp$ collisions collected at $\sqrt{s} = 7 \text{ TeV}$ by the LHCb detector. This result establishes a competitive upper limit on the branching fraction for the decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, which is critical for testing the consistency of the Standard Model.

Symbolic execution is a promising technique for uncovering software bugs, yet scaling it to large-scale systems remains challenging due to issues with state explosion and resource demands. This paper introduces a novel test-guided distributed symbolic execution method designed to mitigate these challenges. The approach employs a "test-depth" partitioning strategy to divide the execution workload, which significantly enhances both efficiency and the ability to detect deep-seated bugs. We developed a test selection algorithm to optimize the order in which tests are processed, thereby maximizing the discovery of critical issues. Additionally, we implemented a distributed symbolic execution engine that integrates this selection algorithm with the partitioning logic. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves substantial gains in both efficiency and the depth of bug detection.

We examine the relaxation dynamics of magnetic dipole interactions within arrays of single-domain ferromagnetic particles. By utilizing a mean-field approach, we derive the characteristic time scale for magnetization relaxation and calculate the corresponding time-dependent hysteresis loop. Our findings indicate that the magnetization relaxation process is governed by a competition between the magnetization's inertia and the strength of the dipole field.

Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning approach that enables clients to train models locally while sharing only model updates with a central server, thereby safeguarding data privacy. However, this reliance on a central server creates a single point of failure and introduces significant communication overhead. To address these limitations, this paper introduces the concept of a "server-free" FL framework, where models are exchanged directly between clients. We further propose a novel, trust-based, server-less FL architecture designed for social networks, where the trust relationships among participants replace the central server. This approach leverages the topology of the social graph to facilitate trust-based model sharing, effectively eliminating the need for centralized coordination. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the system's security and performance characteristics, along with specific protocols for both network initialization and model exchange. Experimental results demonstrate that this server-less design achieves comparable accuracy to traditional FL systems while significantly reducing the system's dependency on centralized infrastructure.

Short-text classification, such as classifying tweets, presents significant challenges for standard deep learning models due to their limited word counts, which often fail to provide sufficient context for accurate prediction. To address this, we introduce a sequential framework designed to handle short text sequences by leveraging historical context. This approach utilizes Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) to capture local and long-term dependencies, respectively. We evaluate our method on the 2013 and 2014 Twitter datasets for political party classification, comparing our results against baseline models including Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machines, and various deep learning architectures. The experiments demonstrate that our sequential framework significantly outperforms the individual RNN and CNN models as well as the standalone baselines.

This study presents a closed-form, analytical model designed to describe the transmission characteristics of telecentric etalons, which are critical components in numerous optical instruments. Unlike previous approaches that relied on iterative methods, this proposed framework is non-iterative, enabling rapid computation of transmission curves. The model's validity is confirmed through comparisons with both simulations and experimental data. Furthermore, this analytical tool offers a streamlined method for characterizing telecentric etalons, which in turn facilitates the optimization of diverse optical devices.

A collection of $k$ matchings in a graph $G$ is defined as compatible provided that the union of any pair constitutes a matching. This paper presents the first polynomial-time algorithm capable of determining the maximum size of the compatible matching set for a given graph $G$. Additionally, we establish a connection between compatible matchings and the concept of a linear forest—a union of paths and cycles. Specifically, we demonstrate that any linear forest with $k$ components can be decomposed into $O(k)$ compatible matchings. This decomposition yields a near-optimal solution for approximating the problem of finding the largest compatible matching set.

The Codelet Model offers a framework for simulating large, parallel systems by utilizing simplified agents called "codelets." This paper examines the relationship between Codelet Models and modern heterogeneous chiplet architectures, proposing a formal mapping from one to the other. We demonstrate that this mapping is highly efficient, with simulations of large-scale chiplet systems running in near-linear time relative to the system's size.

Mixture cure models are widely utilized in medical research to quantify the proportion of cured individuals among those with chronic diseases. A significant limitation of existing literature is its reliance on a two-stage estimation method, which often yields less efficient results than necessary. To address this, we introduce a semiparametric version of the standard two-component mixture cure model, designed to handle censored data. We develop an efficient estimator for the cure fraction using a Gaussian process presmoothing technique to handle the nuisance components. We further demonstrate the asymptotic properties of this estimator, showing that it achieves the optimal efficiency bound. We also provide a simulation study confirming the superior performance of our method compared to current approaches, along with a real-data analysis to illustrate the practical application of our methodology.

In graph theory, a resolving set is defined as a collection of vertices where, for any distinct pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, their respective distances to vertices within the set form unique distance vectors. A set with this property that contains the minimum possible number of vertices is termed a "resolving set," and its cardinality is known as the graph's metric dimension. This metric dimension serves as a measure of a graph's intrinsic metric structure. Conversely, a "non-contradictory" or "non-contradictory" set is defined here as a collection of vertices where, for any distinct pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, their shortest path lengths to vertices within the set are identical only if those paths are identical. A set with this property that contains the minimum possible number of vertices is termed a "non-contradictory set," and its size is known as the graph's "non-contradictory dimension." This paper introduces the concept of "non-contradictory metric dimension" for graphs, which is a generalization of the classical metric dimension. We provide several results regarding the non-contradictory metric dimension of various graph classes, including paths, cycles, complete graphs, complete bipartite graphs, grids, and more.

In-memory computing (IMC) offers significant advantages over traditional von Neumann architectures by mitigating the von Neumann bottleneck and reducing data movement. However, these architectures are susceptible to side-channel attacks, which can leak sensitive data and compromise system security. This paper investigates the specific vulnerabilities of IMC systems by analyzing the power consumption of both resistive and ferroelectric RAM technologies during arithmetic operations. The study reveals that power consumption patterns are highly dependent on the specific operation being executed, the value of the operands, and the resulting output. Consequently, the research demonstrates that an attacker can recover operands and results by monitoring power usage and analyzing the characteristics of the operations performed.

Seismic data frequently suffers from noise, which hampers the extraction of subsurface geological details. While numerous techniques exist to mitigate this issue, they often demand substantial computational resources and extensive manual tuning. This study introduces a novel, self-supervised deep learning framework designed to eliminate noise from seismic traces without requiring manual parameter tuning. The approach leverages blind-spot denoising, a concept rooted in independent component analysis, by training a neural network to reconstruct a specific input channel using only the remaining channels. This methodology effectively isolates and removes noise affecting the target trace. The proposed algorithm utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) that transfers knowledge from a pre-trained model. The findings demonstrate that this technique achieves a significant reduction in noise levels, yielding cleaner seismic data.

This study examines charge asymmetry in lepton-proton elastic scattering, specifically within the framework of one-real-photon emission. By utilizing the laboratory frame, our derived analytical formulas for differential cross-sections offer a straightforward method for calculating this phenomenon. We demonstrate that the charge asymmetry is governed by a ratio of charge factors, which can be expressed solely through the scattering angles of the photon and the lepton (or antilepton). Furthermore, our results are compared with the established charge asymmetry in electron-proton deep inelastic scattering.

The spin-orbit-coupling-driven Mott insulator Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ is a promising candidate for spin-orbit entangled magnetism. This study employs scanning tunneling spectroscopy to investigate its electronic structure, revealing a complex spectrum characterized by spin-polaron bands. This spectral signature arises from the interplay between spin-orbit coupling and the Kondo effect, which is triggered by interactions between the insulator's spins and the conduction electrons in SrIrO$_3$. These findings offer new insights into the nature of spin-orbit entangled magnetism in this class of materials.

The causal mediation effect (CME) quantifies the impact of an exposure on an outcome that is transmitted exclusively through a mediator. While recent literature has extensively explored identification and estimation of the CME under conditions of point identification, it frequently overlooks scenarios where the parameter is non-point identified. This paper addresses a robust identification framework for the CME within a causal mediation model featuring a continuous exposure, focusing on cases where the parameter cannot be point identified. We introduce a multiply robust estimation approach that remains valid under either correct specification of the exposure–mediator–outcome relationships or a valid bounding assumption. Additionally, we develop a double robust method for the CME, demonstrating its consistency, asymptotic normality, and convergence rates. We further establish a double robust outcome-based estimation technique for the CME, proving its consistency, asymptotic normality, and convergence rates. Finally, we apply these methods to analyze the direct effect in the context of continuous exposures. Simulation studies confirm that our proposed methods achieve superior finite sample performance compared to existing approaches.

Identifying suicidal individuals through social media is a critical endeavor for suicide prevention. Although prior research has established that linguistic patterns in online posts can effectively signal suicide risk, the scarcity of large-scale, publicly available datasets containing both text and verified suicide status has hindered progress. To address this, we introduce Robin, a new corpus comprising 1.2 million posts from Twitter accounts confirmed to have died by the end of 2019, along with 1.2 million posts from randomly selected control accounts. Robin is the largest public corpus of its kind, offering a balanced mix of verified cases and controls. Our experiments demonstrate that standard suicide prediction models achieve significantly higher accuracy on Robin compared to other datasets, a result we attribute to Robin's superior balance across classes.

By treating this theory as a topological twist of a two-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=(2,2)$ superconformal field theory, we formulate a topological quantum mechanics featuring both bosonic and fermionic supercharges. The resulting theory possesses a massive vacuum degeneracy characterized by two supermultiplets, with massless states identified as the super-Schwarzian and its superpartner. This framework offers a new perspective on the holographic correspondence between $\mathcal{M}_{1/2}$ and the massive $\mathcal{N}=4$ super-Yang-Mills theory on $S^5$.

We analyze the solutions' global behavior, including boundedness, periodicity, and convergence, presenting sufficient conditions for each phenomenon.

Our analysis reveals that the resulting spacetime geometry is entirely determined by the Born-Infeld parameter, a finding that indicates these solutions serve as a unifying model capable of describing both the Born-Infeld and MacDowell-Mansouri electrodynamics contexts.

This study examines the finite-temperature scaling of the magnetic susceptibility and geometric phase within the spin-1/2 XY chain, a model known for exhibiting a quantum phase transition between a paramagnetic and a ferromagnetic phase. We demonstrate that the magnetic susceptibility's geometric phase component follows a universal scaling law at criticality, which is established through numerical simulations. Additionally, we identify that the finite-temperature behavior of the susceptibility itself is governed by a universal scaling function, a finding supported by both analytical calculations and further numerical verification.

We conducted Monte Carlo simulations on the Ising model to examine the magnetization dynamics during the normal and large-k kinetic mean-field (KMF) quench processes. Our findings indicate that the relaxation times for both initial and final states are governed by the KMF duration, $\tau$, and the temperature of the quench origin ($T_i$). Specifically, the relaxation time of the initial state follows $\tau_i \propto \tau$, while the relaxation time of the final state adheres to $\tau_f \propto \tau^2$. These results align with the predictions of the kinetic mean-field theory. Furthermore, we observed that the system's magnetization evolution during the quench is independent of the quenching speed, provided the KMF time remains sufficiently long.

We examine the localization characteristics of two-particle states within a one-dimensional quasicrystal featuring power-law hopping. Our findings indicate that, regardless of the specific quasiperiodicity sequence, the system exhibits localization for pair separations exceeding a critical distance that scales inversely with the power-law exponent. Furthermore, we observe that the system's behavior is highly sensitive to the arrangement of lattice sites, even when the pair separation remains constant.

Task-Oriented Dialogue (TOD) systems are designed to interact with users to achieve specific goals, such as booking flights or ordering food. Although recent strides in multilingual and cross-lingual models have enhanced their capabilities, these systems still face significant hurdles in accurately understanding and responding to user queries across different languages. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the current state of research in multilingual TOD, highlighting the most effective methodologies for developing such systems. We examine two primary approaches: task-oriented dialogue models utilizing neural machine translation (NMT) and those leveraging pre-trained language models (PLMs). Our analysis indicates that PLM-based frameworks currently outperform NMT-based ones in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, we outline the essential components for constructing a multilingual TOD system, including data preprocessing, model selection, and evaluation metrics. We conclude by discussing the remaining challenges and potential future directions for this field.

Alternative splicing (AS) is a vital gene expression mechanism that generates multiple transcript variants from a single pre-mRNA, with its regulation occurring at various levels, including splicing kinetics. This study investigates the short-term regulatory dynamics of AS by analyzing the temporal expression patterns of numerous transcript isoforms. We introduce a novel approach that integrates differential expression data with co-expression networks to identify splicing events differentially regulated across conditions. This method successfully detects differential regulation in splicing events that were previously overlooked. Furthermore, we observe that co-regulated AS events often cluster within the same gene, suggesting that such events are not merely stochastic occurrences but are likely coordinated through a regulatory mechanism. This finding is supported by a correlation between the number of differentially regulated events and the gene's co-expression network topology. Additionally, we observe that genes exhibiting differential AS regulation are enriched in specific functional categories, indicating a potential link between AS and the regulation of biological processes. This research underscores the importance of considering AS regulation in the context of gene co-expression networks.

The growing importance of data privacy has driven organizations to adopt security and privacy technical controls, yet the specific impact of these controls on data privacy compliance remains unclear. To address this gap, we conducted a qualitative study involving 14 data privacy practitioners. Our findings reveal that data privacy compliance is a complex, multi-step process that does not guarantee the successful adoption of privacy measures. Specifically, organizations often prioritize compliance over deploying privacy controls, and the controls that are implemented do not always align with data privacy regulations. Furthermore, the degree of privacy compliance varies depending on the type of technical control used, indicating that a one-size-fits-all approach does not apply. Consequently, organizations must carefully evaluate the degree of privacy compliance and the specific requirements of their data privacy regulations when selecting and implementing privacy technical controls.

We investigate multiparticle azimuthal angular correlations in $pA$ collisions using the Color Glass Condensate framework. By analyzing the dependence of these correlations on transverse momentum, we demonstrate that the $n$-particle azimuthal power spectrum can be decomposed into two distinct components: a $n$-particle contribution arising from hard scattering and a term representing $1$-particle effects. We contend that this latter component, which is independent of $n$, serves as the primary indicator of final-state effects. Furthermore, our analysis of the $n$-particle azimuthal power spectrum in $pA$ systems reveals that it is dominated by the $n$-particle term, thereby precluding the identification of final-state effects through current measurements.

Furthermore, the ratios of these light nuclei ($d/p$ and $^3$He/d) are found to be independent of both the nuclear mass number ($A$) and collision centrality, indicating that they are governed by the same fundamental production process.

This chapter examines the atmospheric characteristics of rocky exoplanets, with a specific focus on those that are tidally locked. We explore the formation and evolution of their atmospheres, analyzing atmospheric escape, wind dynamics, and thermal redistribution. Furthermore, we address the challenges in modeling these systems, discuss the prospects for observing them, and highlight key questions that remain unresolved.

We investigate the power spectrum of primordial perturbations within the framework of ultra-slow-roll (USR) inflation, incorporating backreaction effects. Our findings indicate that when backreaction is taken into account, the amplitude of the scalar power spectrum is significantly suppressed. This suppression mechanism offers a potential explanation for the observed low value of the spectral index ($s_l$) in the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Furthermore, we demonstrate that the amplitude of the scalar power spectrum can be enhanced by up to 100 times relative to the scenario where backreaction is neglected.

This research addresses the "refined assortment optimization" problem, which involves selecting an optimal product offering from a catalog to maximize expected revenue, subject to the constraint that customers must be able to purchase a subset of at least one product within their preferred bundles. This constraint distinguishes it from traditional assortment optimization, where customers are limited to buying a single item. We propose a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves a constant-factor approximation of the optimal solution, applicable to various demand models, including the Multinomial Logit (MNL) model, the Nested Logit (NL) model, and the Generalized Nested Logit (GNL) model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the refined assortment optimization problem is NP-hard under the MNL model, a result that extends to the NL and GNL frameworks. Finally, we present a polynomial-time approximation scheme (APX) for the NL model, which yields a constant-factor approximation for the GNL model as well.

Survival analysis is a statistical method used to model the time until a specific event occurs, commonly applied in clinical trials to evaluate treatment efficacy. This paper introduces an alternative framework for survival analysis that offers a more intuitive understanding of the topic and simplifies the estimation and comparison of event rates. We also outline a novel approach for estimating confidence intervals for hazard ratios, designed to enhance performance when sample sizes are limited.

We examine a specific category of five-point, five-dimensional, five-loop integrals, which are characterized by a dimensionless form and feature propagators that depend on the external mass scales. This class of integrals is essential for achieving next-to-leading order precision in the calculation of the Higgs-strahlung process ($e^+e^- \to Zh$) at a linear collider. We demonstrate that these integrals can be resolved using the differential equations method.

The surge in electric vehicle (EV) adoption has spurred significant interest in integrating EV charging into existing public parking systems. This paper introduces an online admission control mechanism designed for such infrastructure, enabling parking operators to accept EV requests in real-time without prior knowledge of future demands. The approach relies on a greedy strategy that maximizes charging revenue while strictly adhering to operational limits, such as the total available power capacity. We establish a theoretical upper bound on the competitive ratio of this greedy method, demonstrating that it performs within a constant factor of the optimal offline solution, regardless of specific charging request sequences. Furthermore, the study includes extensive numerical simulations to validate the proposed model and assess its efficacy.

This paper investigates the existence of linear codes over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ that are both self-orthogonal and contain no isotropic vectors. Such codes, known as self-dual and anisotropic codes, are defined by the requirement that their defining bilinear form be both non-degenerate and anisotropic. We establish both necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of these codes and demonstrate that they exist whenever $q$ is an odd prime power and the field dimension $n$ satisfies specific modular constraints. Furthermore, we present an algorithmic method for constructing such codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$, utilizing them to generate explicit examples of anisotropic codes. Finally, we apply these constructions to the study of self-dual codes over finite fields, deriving new results on their existence and construction.

We demonstrate that the leading-order classical scattering amplitudes for any number of massless scalars, photons, and gravitons can be derived from a specific subset of loop integrands within their quantum counterparts. This selection criterion is defined by the absence of massless internal propagators. Our findings indicate that these pure-gravity integrands are sufficient to describe the entire classical behavior, as all additional terms featuring internal propagators contribute only to quantum corrections. This finding represents a significant extension of prior work established for gauge theories.

The decarbonization of the U.S. power sector is essential for meeting national climate objectives, yet it necessitates substantial infrastructure development. This study examines the land-use trade-offs inherent in the American West's electricity decarbonization, specifically focusing on renewable energy expansion. We find that solar photovoltaic (PV) and wind energy projects are predominantly sited in areas with low land values, predominantly rural regions. Our analysis indicates that while these installations can be located on marginal lands, they would displace agricultural activities and degrade ecologically significant habitats. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the projected increase in land consumption for renewable energy by 2050 is significantly higher than current estimates.

Cluster-randomized trials (CRDs) are frequently employed to evaluate vaccine efficacy, particularly when vaccines are administered to entire households. In such studies, the primary unit of randomization is the household, while the individual is the target for vaccination. This setup introduces correlation among individuals within the same household, creating challenges for estimating vaccine effects. This paper examines the estimation of vaccine effects in CRDs where households are randomized and individuals are vaccinated. We propose four distinct estimands: the intention-to-treat (ITT) effect, the individual-level (or direct) effect, the total effect, and the indirect (or herd) effect. We introduce a novel framework for analyzing these estimands, which accounts for the household-level randomization and the resulting intra-household correlation. This framework accommodates various mechanisms of person-to-person transmission and allows for the estimation of vaccine efficacy against transmission. We also present a new method for estimating the indirect effect, termed the "per-exposed" effect, which offers a distinct advantage over the standard indirect effect estimator. This new method is robust to differential loss to follow-up and the presence of unmeasured confounding. We provide a simulation study to evaluate the performance of the proposed estimators and estimands. Finally, we apply the proposed framework to analyze data from a recent randomized trial of a new influenza vaccine.

This study examines the spectral properties of fractal M\"obius Q-maps, specifically the normalized Laplacian spectrum within the context of q-Mobius Q_oct. We establish that the eigenvalues of fractal M\"obius Q_map are derived from the square roots of the Ritz values of a specific matrix. Furthermore, we calculate the eigenvalues of the spectrum for the map and determine its largest and smallest values. We also calculate its Ritz values and provide an explicit formula for its polynomial. Finally, we apply these findings to determine its fractional dimension and calculate its spectral radius.

In distributed contextual bandits, agents operate within an overarching environment where each receives a context vector and a private observation, yet the context vector itself remains inaccessible to other agents. This setup models scenarios like autonomous vehicles navigating a city, where each unit perceives its own local state and signal but cannot observe the states or actions of its peers. This research addresses the distributed linear bandit problem under these constraints, specifically examining scenarios where agents must learn a shared reward function despite not observing each other's context vectors. We propose a novel algorithm that enables agents to collaboratively estimate the global reward function with high accuracy. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the resulting regret grows at a rate of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$, where $T$ represents the time horizon and $K$ denotes the number of arms.

Synthesizing electronic health records (EHR) is a critical technique for protecting patient privacy while enabling the sharing of sensitive data. Although current methods have shown promise, they often fail to capture the intricate relationships between patient attributes and medical diagnoses. This paper introduces a novel approach designed specifically to retain these complex correlations during the anonymization process. We applied this method to cystic fibrosis data, utilizing a probabilistic model to generate synthetic datasets that mirror the real-world statistical properties. Our results demonstrate that the synthetic records closely resemble actual patient data, with a notable improvement in the fidelity of the recorded attribute-diagnosis relationships.

This study examines the decay chain $D^0 \to K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\pm \pi^\mp$ by analyzing the invariant mass distributions of the $K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\pm \pi^\mp$ system and the intermediate $K^\mp \pi^\pm$ pairs. The analysis utilizes a data sample of $1.0 \times 10^9$ $B^0 \to D^{*+}K^-$ decays, where $D^{*+} \to D^0 \pi^+$, collected by the BESIII detector. The data were recorded at a center-of-mass energy of 3.773 GeV, corresponding to the $\psi(3770)$ resonance. The observed signal yields for the $K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\pm \pi^\mp$ final state are $1.0 \times 10^6$ for the $K^-\pi^+\pi^+\pi^-$ mode and $0.8 \times 10^6$ for the $K^+\pi^-\pi^-\pi^-$ mode. Novelpy is a Python package designed to calculate the metrics novelty and disruptiveness for both bibliometric and patent datasets using the concepts of citation velocity and acceleration. These measures quantify how a specific citation contributes to the emergence of new intellectual fields, with novelty and disruptiveness serving as complementary indicators: high disruptiveness denotes the breaking of established patterns, whereas high novelty signifies the creation of new ones. The package offers functions to compute these metrics, generate visualizations, and perform data preprocessing. Novelty and disruptiveness are particularly valuable for evaluating emerging research trends and identifying breakthrough studies. The package is available on GitHub and includes a user-friendly interface.

This paper investigates the potential for a humanoid robot to shoot an Olympic recurve bow. We examined the challenges associated with the necessary motor skills, including bow preparation, aiming, and drawing, and assessed the feasibility of executing these tasks using a KUKA IIWA robot. Additionally, we developed a simulation environment to model the physics of the equipment and demonstrated a successful test where the robot successfully released an arrow.

Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has become a significant challenge in recommender systems, aiming to predict user preferences for target domains using data from source domains. While existing CDR methods typically rely on learning shared user/item embeddings to transfer knowledge, they often overlook the distinct characteristics of the source and target domains. This oversight can lead to negative transfer, where irrelevant information hinders performance. To address this, we introduce Dual Metric Learning (DML), a new framework that explicitly accounts for domain differences by employing distinct metric learning objectives for each domain. DML consists of two components: a dual metric learning (DML) objective that jointly optimizes both domains, and a dual contrastive learning (DCL) objective that learns separate embedding spaces. This dual-space approach allows the system to capture domain-specific nuances while maintaining shared representations. We further enhance efficiency by applying a novel pruning strategy that significantly reduces the number of embedding parameters without sacrificing accuracy. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that DML outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving substantial gains in recommendation quality. Additionally, our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the proposed pruning technique.

We demonstrate that the modal mu-calculus fragment known as the mu-fraction—defined by excluding nested fixpoints—is precisely the language of asynchronous distributed automata. These structures consist of finite-state machines where transitions are governed by the mu-calculus, but the state space is infinitely distributed and coordinated via a shared partial order. This result extends previous findings regarding the semantics of the mu-fraction, originally established for distributed automata in [Bartocci et al., LICS 2019].

This study examines the thermal conductivity of a 2D complex plasma characterized by anions with strong correlations and weakly interacting positive ions. The analysis focuses on the 2DX geometry, where the positive ions form a rigid lattice and the negative ions occupy a 2D fluid phase. The temperature-dependent thermal conductivity of the anions was calculated using the Green-Kubo relation, employing molecular dynamics simulations. The findings indicate that thermal conductivity increases with temperature, aligning with theoretical predictions for a strongly coupled one-dimensional Yukawa fluid. Furthermore, the study establishes that the temperature dependence of thermal conductivity is governed by the system's coupling parameter.

This study examines the problem of determining whether a target vector $\mathbf{v}$ can be expressed as a sum of unordered data vectors from a given set $V$, where each vector in $V$ contains non-negative integers. We demonstrate that this problem is NP-complete by establishing a reduction from the Subset Sum problem. Furthermore, we analyze the issue within a specific context involving vectors of equal length, offering a polynomial-time algorithm for this scenario.

Cardio-angiography (CAG) is a critical diagnostic tool for identifying coronary artery disease, yet it carries a significant risk of ionizing radiation exposure. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to reduce such exposure by intelligently interpolating cardiac angiography video frames. Utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN) for feature extraction and a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) for reconstruction, our approach synthesizes intermediate frames from existing ones. We evaluated the method using both simulated and real-world video datasets, comparing performance against a baseline of linear interpolation. Results demonstrate that our model achieves superior PSNR and SSIM scores, producing more natural video sequences. Furthermore, we validated the technique on actual CAG data, confirming that our method maintains diagnostic image quality suitable for clinical use.

The FCC-ee, a proposed future electron-positron collider, is designed to operate at center-of-mass energies of 90, 116.5, 133, 140, 150, 1000, and 10000 GeV, with projected luminosities ranging from $10^{34}$ to $10^{36}$ fb$^{-1}$. This facility will enable the study of heavy-quark bound states and their associated excited resonances. This overview outlines the primary physics goals concerning heavy-quark states and their theoretical predictions, while also highlighting the associated challenges.

This study examines the cosmological implications of leptophilic $U(1)$ gauge symmetries featuring $L_\mu - L_\tau$, $L_{\mu} - L_{\tau} - L_{\tau}$, or $L_{\mu} - L_{\tau} - L_{\tau} - L_{\tau}$ charges. We demonstrate that the presence of these gauge symmetries induces a new energy scale, $T'$, which significantly alters the universe's thermal history. This shift in temperature alters the standard cosmological timeline, resulting in a modified freeze-out temperature for relic neutrinos. We find that the relic neutrino density is substantially reduced compared to predictions from the standard model, establishing a new neutrino floor at $Y_{\nu} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-6}$. This finding holds true for the specific gauge symmetries analyzed, including $U(1)_{L_\mu - L_\tau}$, $U(1)_{L_\mu - L_\tau - L_\tau}$, and $U(1)_{L_\mu - L_\tau - L_\tau - L_\tau}$, and we also discuss the broader cosmological implications of these gauge symmetries.

The gravitational influence of a massive companion on a star's orbit can cause significant secular perturbations, potentially leading to the star's ejection from the host system. This paper investigates the likelihood of such an ejection occurring when a star is perturbed by an intermediate-mass companion (IMC) within the strong tidal field of the Galactic Center (GC). We find that while the probability of ejection is negligible for IMCs with masses below 100 M☉, it becomes significant for IMCs with masses between 100 and 1000 M☉. The most probable ejection mechanism involves a Kozai-Lidov cycle, where the IMC induces secular variations in the star's orbital eccentricity and inclination, driving the star to collide with the GC's central black hole. This process is highly sensitive to the IMC's mass, the initial orbital parameters of the star, and the spatial distribution of IMCs. Our analysis indicates that IMCs with masses between 100 and 1000 M☉ could account for the observed hypervelocity stars (HVSs) in the Milky Way, provided that the IMCs are distributed within a few parsecs of the GC.

This paper examines multistep stochastic differential equations (SDEs) driven by multiplicative noise, where the martingale measure exhibits singularity relative to Lebesgue measure. We establish the existence of weak solutions for a class of nonlinear SDEs with polynomial drift and diffusion coefficients, even when global solutions fail to exist. This proof leverages the regularity provided by specific noise, utilizing a family of linear equations that closely resemble the original nonlinear system but with smoothed drift terms. By applying Frechet differentiability to the solution mapping connecting these linearized solutions to the corresponding nonlinear solution, we derive probabilistic weighted bounds for derivatives of the nonlinear system. These findings are instrumental in demonstrating the existence of weak solutions for the target SDEs.

We demonstrate that the ideal $NS_{\omega_1}$ is $\omega_2$-generically null within any model containing a supercompact cardinal, implying that $\sf MM_{\omega + 1}$ precludes the definability of the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$. Furthermore, we show that the nonstationary ideal on $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$ is $\mathcal{P}(\omega)$-generically null whenever the model satisfies a version of the forcing axiom involving $\omega_2$-closed forcing.

Although pretraining on vast datasets is standard for language models, this approach often leads to suboptimal performance on downstream tasks. To address this, we introduce Adaptor, a framework that trains a lightweight adapter on a specific objective to generate new tokens that implicitly encode the objective. This design allows the model to retain its original pretraining capabilities while requiring only a minimal number of parameters to adapt to new tasks. We further develop a novel objective called *Adaptor Prompting*, which functions as a generalization of next-token prediction by focusing on predicting the completion of prompts that have been specifically adapted to a target task. We demonstrate that adaptor significantly outperforms existing methods, including those using prompt-tuning objectives, on various benchmarks. Notably, the framework achieves state-of-the-art results on the GLUE benchmark using the 110M DeBERTa model and matches the performance of the GPT-2 large model with just 1.5M parameters.

This paper introduces the Mapillary Traffic Sign Dataset, comprising over 100,000 images of traffic signs captured globally by individual smartphone users via street-level contributions. The collection contains 133 distinct sign categories, with annotations performed by human experts. We provide baseline performance metrics for both traffic sign detection and classification using the dataset. Additionally, we have released the dataset to the public, accompanied by a detailed guide on sign categories and a summary of annotation methods.

Collaborative filtering (CF) has long been a cornerstone of recommender systems, with deep learning methods gaining significant traction in recent years. However, deep CF models typically depend on pre-trained item embeddings, which are often generated by item-item CF algorithms. This paper introduces SelfCF, a new self-supervised CF framework that eliminates the need for external pre-training. By utilizing a self-supervised strategy to derive item embeddings directly from user-item interactions, SelfCF achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets. Additionally, it demonstrates the ability to effectively handle cold-start item challenges.

Tevelev morphisms, which are particular types of maps from moduli spaces of coverings to those of target curves, have been the subject of extensive research. This study broadens the definition of these morphisms to include cases where the branching data is non-zero at every marked point. We compute the generalized Tevelev degrees for $\mathbb{P}^1$ by leveraging the duality between moduli spaces of $\mathbb{P}^1$ and $\mathbb{P}^1$-parabolic maps and those of parabolic logarithmic differentials. Furthermore, we establish a recursive formula for these degrees, which facilitates the calculation of values for various configurations.

This study examines a gapped Dirac semimetal characterized by mixed dispersive properties, combining parabolic and linear behaviors. The analysis employs a $2+1$-dimensional massive Dirac model, with dispersion relations along two spatial dimensions being anisotropic: one is linear, the other parabolic. The gap opening is attributed to a scalar mass term. We investigate the topological properties of this system, specifically the phase diagram and the corresponding topological invariants. Furthermore, we analyze the system's behavior under a uniform magnetic field, determining its energy spectrum and examining the topological characteristics of the resulting Landau levels.

This work examines the entry/exit times for a one-dimensional curve evolving under a slow, semi-stable dynamics, specifically within a regime where the particle remains trapped in a halo. We derive precise logarithmic corrections to the polynomial rates of these times, demonstrating that such refinements are essential for accurately characterizing the particle's behavior near the boundaries of this halo.

The findings in this work pertain to an analysis of the entry/and exit durations associated with a one-dimensional curve undergoing slow, semi-stable dynamics, specifically in a context where the particle is confined

Gravitational-wave detectors are uniquely capable of identifying gravitational-wave signals that are otherwise undetectable by electromagnetic observatories. This study examines the detectability of higher-order modes (HoMs) in gravitational-wave signals from compact binary coalescences, specifically targeting events involving spinning, unequal-mass black holes that are expected by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration during its third-generation observing run. We utilize the third-generation sensitivity curves from the Einstein Telescope (ET) and the Cosmic Explorer (CE) to estimate the detectable population of HoM signals. Our results indicate that third-generation detectors will be able to identify HoM signals from these black hole mergers at a rate of approximately 100 to 1000 events per year. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these detectors can resolve the HoM contribution to the total signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for a significant portion of these events, spanning from 10% to 50%. This capability will facilitate the precise measurement of black hole spins and masses, thereby offering new insights into the mechanisms of black hole formation.

This study introduces a novel technique for determining the mass of Gaia satellites by analyzing the astrometric shifts of stars located within their partial orbital paths. Leveraging the substantial number of partial orbits detected by Gaia, the method offers a unique opportunity to measure the mass distribution of these dark, compact objects. We demonstrate the method's validity through simulations, showing that it achieves a precision of approximately 10% for a single object, even with a 10-year dataset. Furthermore, the approach is applied to the first real-world candidate, Gaia 180010100, a black hole identified by the Gaia Black Hole Catalog. We estimate its mass to be $1.9 \pm 0.2 M_{\odot}$, a result consistent with previous findings. We also discuss the method's limitations and outline its future potential for the broader scientific community.

The 0/1 Knapsack problem is a well-known combinatorial optimization challenge that has been widely addressed using Genetic Algorithms (GA). This study evaluates the performance of various GA convergence strategies, specifically comparing different crossover and selection techniques. The analysis covers four selection methods—Roulette Wheel, Tournament, Rank, and Fitness Proportional—combined with either one-point or uniform crossover. Results indicate that the Tournament pairing for selection with one-point crossover yields the superior convergence rate. Conversely, when assessing crossover methods under the Fitness Proportional selection scheme, one-point crossover demonstrates the highest convergence.

This work investigates $L^2$-norm bounds for trilinear oscillatory integrals of a convolution type defined on the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. The result establishes that if the gradients of the respective phases in the $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)$ norm collectively exceed a threshold of $1/2$, then the corresponding multilinear operator is bounded on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$.

This study introduces a hate speech detection system that surpasses the current state-of-the-art, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.959 on the Twitter dataset. The system leverages T5, a state-of-the-art pre-trained Transformer model, enhanced with a custom data augmentation technique. Furthermore, this approach integrates the T5 model with a logistic regression classifier to maximize performance. The T5 model was trained using hate speech data sourced from both the Twiiter and Facebook datasets. To boost the T5 model's efficacy, data augmentation was applied to the training data using back-translation, specifically translating text from English to German and back. The final solution combines the outputs of the T5 model and the logistic regression classifier through a weighted average, utilizing the T5 model's higher confidence scores for its predictions.

We examine the scaling behavior of computational resources required for forces in helium and lithium atoms via the Variational Quantum Algorithm (VQA). Our findings indicate that the number of measurements needed for force estimation scales cubically with the number of qubits, a figure that is lower than the scaling observed for energy calculations. Additionally, we demonstrate that employing a modified Ansatz, which incorporates the exact Coulomb interaction between particles, significantly enhances the signal-to-noise ratio for the estimated forces.

Elections are fundamental to democratic societies, yet the 2020 U.S. presidential race was marred by widespread claims of election fraud. This study introduces a comprehensive, multi-modal dataset comprising 1.2 million tweets related to 2020 U.S. election fraud, featuring both text and audio representations. The collection includes a curated subset of 100,000 claims verified by human experts, alongside a larger pool of 1.1 million non-claim tweets. This resource is intended to facilitate the development of automated detection systems for election fraud claims.

Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) are a promising approach for uncertainty quantification, yet their practical application is hindered by the computational complexity of integrating over their weight space. To address this, we introduce a novel method that encodes the latent posterior of BNN weights into a single, deterministic representation. This representation is designed to be efficiently decoded to produce a neural network capable of generating predictive distributions. We demonstrate that this approach yields more accurate uncertainty estimates than current state-of-the-art techniques, while also offering significant computational efficiency gains.

This study introduces a semiclassical instanton framework for Marcus-type electron transfer theory, where the approach is derived by integrating semiclassical instanton methods with the classical treatment of high-temperature nuclear motion. The resulting expression for the rate aligns with standard Marcus theory, with the activation energy determined by the sign of $\lambda_0$. Specifically, the activation energy is zero when there is no activation (i.e., $\lambda_0 \geq 0$), whereas for $\lambda_0 < 0$, it is expressed as $E_a = \frac{1}{2}(\lambda_0 - \sqrt{\lambda_0^2 - 4\Delta^2})$. The theory also provides explicit formulas for the instanton action and electron-transfer probability density. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this semiclassical instanton formulation yields the correct classical high-temperature limit. The approach is further extended to include Debye and Einstein models for high-temperature nuclear dynamics. Finally, we numerically calculate the instanton action and rate constants for Marcus electron transfer using the semiclassical instanton method and compare these results with full quantum instanton simulations.

This study introduces a hybrid control design methodology for trajectory tracking, which integrates a model predictive control (MPC) scheme with a sliding mode control (SMC) framework. The MPC component generates the primary control signal to ensure precise trajectory following, while the SMC component supplies an auxiliary signal to dampen oscillations and mitigate the MPC's sensitivity to disturbances. This synergistic approach effectively resolves the trade-off between maintaining high tracking accuracy and achieving robustness against uncertainties. Furthermore, the controller employs a novel switching logic based on a predefined hysteresis band to minimize reliance on the SCG component, thereby reducing its impact on the controlled system. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid controller outperforms traditional MPC and pure SCG strategies in terms of tracking accuracy and disturbance rejection capabilities.

The colossal magnetoresistance phenomenon observed in thin-film Heusler alloys is attributed to a magnon drag mechanism. This study demonstrates that magnon drag serves as a fundamental source of the thermoelectric effect, proposing a theoretical framework that aligns with experimental findings in Heusler alloys. The model posits that magnons transfer momentum to conduction electrons, thereby enhancing their mobility. Consequently, the Seebeck coefficient is determined by the disparity between the magnon chemical potential and that of the electrons. Theoretical analysis reveals that magnons impart momentum proportional to their own chemical potential, leading to a Seebeck coefficient that scales linearly with the applied magnetic field. Furthermore, the model predicts a sign reversal in the Seebeck coefficient when the temperature drops below the magnon chemical potential. The proposed theoretical approach offers a viable pathway for achieving high-performance thermoelectric materials.

The Perfect Sum Problem seeks to determine the count of subsets within a set of $n$ positive integers that total exactly $k$. This study introduces a probabilistic algorithm to address this issue, which operates in $O(n \log n)$ time with a high probability of success. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(n \log n)$ for time complexity on deterministic algorithms with a high probability of failure rate.

This work demonstrates that within every finite field $F_{q^n}$ where $F_{q^n}$ has order $q^n$ and $n$ is a square-free integer, there always exists a non-zero element $a$ such that the polynomial $x^n - a$ is irreducible over $F_q$. Furthermore, we show that there is a specific element $a$ for which this polynomial $x^n - a$ is not only irreducible but also represents a higher-order element in $F_{q^n}$, where $n$ is a square-free integer. This result is proven using a method that involves the application of the Chebotarev Density Theorem.

We present a novel methodology for analyzing source code by modeling it as a concurrent system. Within this model, individual program constructs are represented as states, and their interactions are depicted as transitions. These elements are implemented as timed automata, allowing the entire system to be executed on the Uppaal toolset. This environment supports the verification of various system properties, including deadlock detection. This approach is validated through its application to an open-source implementation of the Apache Commons Collections library.

We introduce a novel, end-to-end optimization framework for designing metasurfaces tailored for compressive sensing imaging. This approach integrates the reconstruction algorithm and the optical design process into a unified scheme, allowing for the direct generation of surface profiles that map straight to the final image. By leveraging deep learning's end-to-end capabilities, our method overcomes the limitations of conventional analytical techniques, which often fail to produce optimal results for complex targets. We demonstrate that this strategy excels at recovering images from sparse measurements, even when those measurements are corrupted by noise.

This study examines the ionization of hydrogen under the influence of combined intense, counter-rotating circularly polarized laser fields. Our findings reveal that the ionization rate is modulated by a significant AC-Stark shift, a phenomenon that produces observable sidebands in the electron momentum spectrum. These momentum sidebands correspond to resonant double recombination events, a process where the electron's binding energy is altered by the AC-Stark effect. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these resonances can be controlled by adjusting the relative phase of the two laser fields.

Image-to-image translation is a deep learning technique that converts an input image into a target domain, such as translating a horse into a donkey. While current methods struggle to maintain semantic consistency in the output, we introduce a new approach that generates images where the semantic content of one object (e.g., a horse) is mixed with another (e.g., a donkey). We achieve this by utilizing a pre-trained semantic segmentation model to isolate specific regions of interest, which are then processed through a generative adversarial network (GAN) to create the final mixed result.

Gene expression is inherently stochastic, and stochastic modeling offers a vital framework for deciphering the regulatory mechanisms of gene expression. This study introduces a statistical approach for estimating parameters in stochastic differential equation (SDE) models of gene expression, grounded in the framework of diffusion processes. We establish the asymptotic properties of our method, confirming that the resulting estimates are consistent and follow a Gaussian distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's efficacy through simulations and apply it to analyze the stochastic dynamics of the *lac* operon.

This paper introduces a new data-driven semi-supervised learning framework that integrates the manifold hypothesis with the Siamese Triplet Network (STN) architecture. The proposed method, named semi-supervised data-driven learning (SSDL), utilizes a data-driven manifold regularizer to enhance the STN model. Our experimental results demonstrate that SSDL achieves superior performance compared to the STN baseline and other leading semi-supervised learning techniques.

Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms (QAOA) are quantum machine learning approaches designed to address combinatorial optimization tasks. This study investigates QAOA's performance on the MaxCut problem using a bipartite random graph, focusing on how the number of layers ($p$) and the total number of qubits ($n$) influence the algorithm's ability to reach the optimal solution. We demonstrate that the QAOA's capacity to find the ground state is governed by the ratio $n/p$. Specifically, when this ratio exceeds a critical threshold, the algorithm successfully identifies the optimal solution; conversely, a sub-critical ratio results in a performance gap relative to the optimum. Furthermore, we show that the probability of attaining the optimal state decays exponentially with $p$ for sub-critical conditions. These findings are supported by both analytical proofs and numerical simulations.

Person Re-Identification (Re-ID) is a computer vision task that involves identifying whether a specific individual appears in a different, unseen camera feed. This re-recognition process relies on extracting distinctive features from images of individuals to match them across various viewpoints and environments. The primary challenge in Re-ID stems from the fact that the same person may appear differently across multiple cameras due to factors like lighting, background clutter, and camera angles. Consequently, the system must learn to focus on stable, identity-specific characteristics while disregarding irrelevant visual noise. This paper presents a novel Re-ID framework that leverages a multi-scale feature extraction module alongside a cross-domain attention mechanism to isolate the most relevant person-specific attributes. The proposed approach is evaluated on two prominent public datasets, MS-MARVEL and DukeMTMC-reID, and achieves competitive performance relative to current state-of-the-art methodologies.

Power system research frequently relies on time series data, which is often unavailable due to the high cost of acquiring detailed models. While researchers have previously attempted to synthesize such data using physics-based models, these approaches are frequently inaccurate and fail to capture the complexities of real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a data-driven methodology for time series reconstruction that utilizes machine learning to analyze existing data and generate new, plausible datasets. The study evaluates various reconstruction techniques, including autoencoders, variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks, by comparing their performance in terms of data quality and computational efficiency. The findings indicate that variational autoencoders offer the optimal balance between accuracy and speed, making them highly suitable for power system research. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that these autoencoder-based models can be effectively trained on high-dimensional data, such as power flow results, highlighting their versatility.

This paper examines the strong convergence of solutions to the variational inequality problem (VIP) by employing a nonexpansive operator $T$ within a Hilbert space context. The proposed method involves an iterative process that combines a perturbed fixed-point algorithm with a contraction mapping, specifically designed to compute the unique solution to a given VIP. Furthermore, the work establishes sufficient conditions ensuring the algorithm's strong convergence, while also presenting numerical experiments to validate the proposed approach.

This study investigates the geometric and arithmetic characteristics of isoxial Fuchsian groups, which are characterized by the condition that the shortest geodesic intersecting any geodesic element is unique. We demonstrate that this condition is equivalent to the group being of the first kind, possessing a fundamental domain bounded by exactly three sides, and being associated with an elliptic modulus within the imaginary quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(i)$. Furthermore, we establish the density of such groups among all arithmetic Fuchsian groups and prove that the limit set of an isoxial group is always a circle.

This study reports on an investigation into the lepton flavor-violating decay of $\Upsilon(3S)$ into $e^{\pm}\mu^{\pm}$. Utilizing a data sample of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the Belle detector at the KEKB $e^+e^-$ collider, the analysis establishes upper limits on the branching fractions at a 90% confidence level. Specifically, the constraints are $\mathcal{B}(\Upsilon(3S)\rightarrow e^+\mu^-\leq 1.0\times 10^{-7}$ and $\mathcal{B}(\Upsilon(3S)\rightarrow e^-\mu^+\leq 1.0\times 10^{-7}$.

The discovery of flat-band systems has significantly advanced the study of strongly correlated materials. This study reports the synthesis of Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ compounds with varying Se concentrations ($x$) and demonstrates that their electronic structures are highly sensitive to Se doping. Specifically, the optical conductivity spectra indicate that Se substitution tunes the system from a flat-band regime to a semi-metallic state. Furthermore, under high pressure, the compound with $x=0.75$ exhibits superconductivity with a critical temperature ($T_c$) of 1.5 GPa. These findings suggest that the proximity of the system to a flat-band regime is essential for achieving high-temperature superconductivity.

We investigate the information recovery challenge in two-dimensional Juttner-Lindbladian gravity, demonstrating that the Page time corresponds to the point where the black hole's mass reaches a critical threshold. This transition marks a shift from a negative to a positive value for the cosmological constant. We identify this threshold as the mass at which the black hole horizon touches the bulk spacetime's boundary.

Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) are widely recognized as an effective deep learning architecture for modeling continuous dynamics. However, in real-world scenarios, data is often contaminated by noise, making it impractical to directly apply Neural ODEs. To address this, we introduce a framework that learns the underlying continuous dynamics from noisy observations. We achieve this by integrating a Neural ODE into a latent space, where we optimize the mapping between data and latent representations using a composite loss function. This function combines a data-fitting term, a regularization term, and a regularization term based on the discrepancy between the mapped dynamics and the observed noisy trajectory. Object goal navigation is a critical challenge in robotics, requiring agents to move to specific targets within an unfamiliar setting. This task is difficult because the agent must identify the goal, plan a path while avoiding obstacles, and execute it while continuously verifying proximity to the target. To address this, we introduce the Object Memory Transformer (OMT), a transformer-based memory architecture designed to store and retrieve information about objects in the environment. OMT utilizes a goal-conditioned encoder to create a memory of the scene, which is then processed by a transformer to generate a sequence of object embeddings. These embeddings are used to construct a global map, allowing the agent to locate the goal and generate a high-level trajectory. To handle low-level execution and real-time obstacle avoidance, we employ a reinforcement learning-based low-level controller that takes commands from the high-level system. This hybrid approach is evaluated on the Object Goal Navigation dataset, where it outperforms existing methods.

The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has sparked significant interest in instruction tuning, a method that leverages human-generated instructions to train models to follow commands. However, the prohibitive costs associated with creating such data have driven the development of automated approaches to replace manual annotation. Despite this, current automated techniques often fail to match the performance of human-annotated results. This paper introduces OPT-IML, a novel framework designed to enhance the automatic generation of instructions. OPT-IML operates by first prompting the model to predict the target action and subsequently using the model itself to formulate the instruction based on that prediction. This strategy ensures that OPT-IML produces instructions that are both semantically clear and semantically appropriate, leading to superior model performance. Empirical evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that OPT-IML significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving results comparable to those obtained through human annotation.

This study examines the perturbative energy of the uniform electron gas (UEG) at low densities using the fully optimized Jaszczak and Krawetz transcorrelated (TC) Jastrow trial wave function. Our findings indicate that this TC Jastrow function yields a variational energy that is 0.01 Hartree lower than the conventional Jastrow approach. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the corresponding correlation energy remains 0.1 Hartree more favorable than results from the standard formulation.

This study introduces a new approach to generating physically consistent ensembles for the shallow-water equations, grounded in the theory of optimal transport. By leveraging recent insights into optimal transport, we establish a framework that defines physical constraints for the system's phase space, thereby enabling the construction of invariant sets that bound uncertainty. Our methodology addresses the inherent nonlinearity of these equations, which typically renders the derivation of analytical solutions for uncertainty propagation unfeasible. We demonstrate that the proposed method is both general and effective, successfully encompassing established uncertainty quantification techniques as special cases.

This study introduces a privacy-preserving framework for Big Data analysis that leverages Randomized Tensor Network Decomposition (RTND) combined with Dispersed Tensor Computation (DTC). The methodology operates in two distinct phases: first, RTND transforms the original data into a compact tensor network structure, significantly reducing storage requirements while maintaining the core data semantics. Second, utilizing this framework, the system performs computations on the network in a distributed manner. This allows multiple parties to jointly analyze the data without revealing their individual contributions, as the inherent properties of tensor networks ensure that the results reflect the original data relationships. The paper further details how to generate the necessary RTND structures securely through a multi-party computation protocol. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is validated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets.

Robot learning algorithms, particularly deep neural networks, are highly susceptible to adversarial attacks, which can cause severe safety risks when deployed on physical systems. Current methods for detecting and mitigating these threats are often computationally intensive and unsuitable for real-time applications. To address this, we introduce SafeAPT, a new framework designed to ensure the safe deployment of simulation-trained policies in the real world. SafeAPT operates by first training a broad array of policies in a simulator, each optimized for distinct objectives. These policies are then deployed on the robot, where SafeAPT monitors their performance and selects the most appropriate one dynamically based on the specific task. By leveraging this policy diversity, SafeAPT can identify and prevent adversarial attacks in real-time without the need for complex adversarial training or detection mechanisms. Experimental results demonstrate that SafeAPT successfully blocks adversarial inputs in real-time while maintaining high task performance comparable to the best individual policy.

This study offers a concise overview of the observational characteristics of jets within radio galaxies and quasars, with a specific emphasis on the most luminous quasars. We examine the morphology of jets and their surrounding environments, as well as the structures formed at the jet's termination. Additionally, we analyze the evolution of jets within their host galaxies and the resulting feedback mechanisms. We also explore the connection between jet power and black hole mass, along with the energetic output of jets in relation to the radiated power of their host galaxies.

This paper introduces a time-inhomogeneous nonparametric regression framework designed to analyze nonstationary time series. The proposed estimator utilizes a local sieve approach grounded in a weighted kernel, where weights are tailored to the series' time-dependent characteristics. It is demonstrated that this estimator achieves pointwise consistency and convergence rates that rival those of i.i.d. nonparametric regression methods. Furthermore, the article develops a time-inhomogeneous sieve inference test, employing a local adaptive lasso technique to identify significant lags dynamically. Simulation results indicate that the estimator performs effectively in scenarios with moderate to strong nonstationarity, while an application to U.S. quarterly GDP data demonstrates the method's utility in detecting time-varying lags and quantifying how their significance evolves over time.

This study investigates the efficacy of neural architectures for identifying offensive language in text, utilizing the Paraphrase-MiniBoGe dataset. We compare a recurrent neural network (RNN) with a transformer model, evaluating their performance through accuracy, F1 scores, and the use of attention visualizations. Our findings indicate that, contrary to expectations, the RNN outperforms the transformer in this specific task. We conclude that RNNs are better suited for this application and demonstrate that attention visualizations can effectively reveal the key features contributing to an rnn's classification decisions.

This paper introduces a novel application of dissipative theory to the study of Nesterov's accelerated method, a renowned algorithm for convex optimization. We demonstrate that specific system behaviors associated with this accelerated method align with the core principles of dissipative theory. Leveraging these properties, we derive a straightforward proof of the algorithm's convergence, a result originally established by Alex Nesterov.

The method employs a fictitious domain approach, treating the boundary region as a computational void. By deriving the optimal solution for this void space, the boundary conditions are enforced effectively. The proposed scheme is validated through two test cases: the flow around a cylinder and the lid-driven cavity problem.

The paper introduces credal valuation networks (CVNs), which represent the credal set using a specific valuation function. This approach offers a more compact representation of credal sets compared to standard methods like Bayesian networks, imprecise probabilistic networks, or lexicographic ordering. The authors demonstrate that CVNs support efficient algorithms for computing optimal decisions and performing inference. Furthermore, they show that CVNs can be derived from various valuation types through a specific credal ordering, enabling efficient credal set construction and providing a unified framework for diverse uncertainty sources. The authors also establish that CVNs can be extended to handle uncertain evidence, resulting in CVNs with evidence. Finally, the paper highlights the practical utility of CVNs through application to machine reasoning under uncertainty, specifically in natural language processing.

Top-K recommendation has become a standard approach in modern recommender systems. While traditional methods rely on point estimation, Probabilistic Metric Learning (PML) offers a superior alternative by modeling the uncertainty inherent in user-item interactions. This study introduces a novel PML framework for top-K recommendation that integrates a margin-based loss function to enhance the separation between similar and dissimilar items. Specifically, the proposed method employs a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to estimate the probability density of user-item interactions and derives the optimal margin dynamically from the top-K item scores for each user. Empirical evaluations on two real-world datasets demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines.

Quantum channels are often modeled as memoryless, Markovian processes, yet this assumption fails when significant correlations exist between sequential operations. In this work, we demonstrate that the "eternal non-Markovianity" of a channel—meaning it remains non-Markovian regardless of how many times it is repeated—is the definitive criterion for such persistent non-Markovian behavior. We establish that a non-unital channel exhibits this property if and only if it is either entangle-breaking or fully entangle-degrading. Furthermore, we derive a specific necessary and sufficient condition for a channel to be fully entangle-degrading.

This study introduces a novel framework for efficient classification that leverages counterfactual reasoning and active learning. The proposed method, termed Active Learning with Counterfactual Reasoning (ALCR), utilizes a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) to synthesize counterfactual data points. These synthetic samples are then employed to predict labels for unlabeled instances. The framework is designed to minimize the quantity of training data required for label prediction. Experimental evaluations on the Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that ALCR achieves superior performance compared to existing active learning approaches.

Robotic Simulated Environments (RSEs) are widely utilized for developing and evaluating autonomous systems, yet their application in assessing semantic mapping algorithms remains underexplored. This paper introduces the Robotic Simulated Environment for Evaluation and Benchmarking of Semantic Mapping (RoSmEEry), a new RSE designed specifically for this task. RoSmEEry offers a comprehensive suite of tools, including a simulator, a dataset generator, and a visualization module, enabling users to create and test semantic mapping algorithms. The system integrates a physics engine for realistic object dynamics, a LiDAR sensor model, and a semantic segmentation library. We provide the dataset generator to produce customizable environments and offer a visual tool to aid in the analysis of generated data. Additionally, we present a specific RoSmEEry scenario and a baseline semantic mapping algorithm for validation. Experimental results demonstrate that this baseline algorithm achieves a 97.5% mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) score on the provided dataset.

Rikudo, a two-player impartial game, is analyzed in this paper. It is demonstrated that determining the winner of a Rikudo instance is an NP-complete problem. The Rikudo problem shares the same computational complexity classification as several other path-based games, including the classic Nim, as well as the path variants known as Path, Switch, and Switch.
