This study examines the approximation error of a Hankel Sobolev function using Prolate Spheroidal Wave Functions (P.S.Fs) on a circular domain. The error analysis relies on the spectral properties of a compact self-adjoint operator, $\mathcal{K}$, which is defined by a kernel $K(x,y)$ that is square integrable with respect to the Lebesgue measure on the unit disk. The results demonstrate that the approximation error is bounded by the product of the singular values of the operator, $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, where $\sigma_1 > \sigma_2 > 0$, multiplied by the Hankel Sobolev norm of the function.

This study introduces a novel approach to identifying atomic structures using a diffusion model grounded in machine learning. The method leverages the score function derived from a learned denoising model to progressively transition an unknown atomic configuration toward one resembling a known reference structure. This process is optimized by minimizing the discrepancy between the generated structure and the target, effectively functioning as a structured refinement technique. We validate this method through computational experiments on two-dimensional square lattices, demonstrating its potential for application in advanced imaging techniques such as cryo-electron microscopy.

This study introduces a new Lagrangian framework designed to analyze transport and mixing within the ocean. By utilizing the Lagrangian mean gradient and curvature, the method identifies coherent structures and their evolution, thereby offering insights into the mechanisms driving water transport. The approach is applied to a two-dimensional numerical model of a coastal current, where it detects and tracks a coherent structure that persists for several weeks. The findings indicate that the structure's longevity is sustained by the combined effects of the mean flow and its associated vorticity.

This study investigates the glass transition in polymer melts using the equation of state (EOS) framework and a theory of entropy scaling. We demonstrate that the Adam-Gibbs equation, which links the glass transition to the relaxation time, can be derived from the free volume theory. Furthermore, we show that the entropy scaling model, which correlates relaxation time with the product of density and specific heat capacity, is mathematically equivalent to the Adam-Gibbs approach. We also discuss the findings in relation to recent research on the thermodynamic scaling model.

This study introduces a semi-discretization of the modified Camassa-Holm equation that includes linear dispersion terms, constructed by applying the Lax pair's semi-discretization technique directly to its associated pair. We demonstrate that this approach maintains the equation's integrability. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of the resulting semi-discretization using both linear and numerical methods. Finally, numerical experiments confirm that the integrative properties of this approach are consistent with those of the continuous model.

This work introduces a new framework for quantum mechanics that extends the de Broglie-Bohm-Bell approach by employing a spinor wavefunction, specifically designed to address the spin-1/2 particle. Within this theory, particle trajectories are defined by a spinor pilot wave. The spin measurement outcomes are derived from the particle's position and the spin of the guiding wave. We demonstrate that this model reproduces the spin-1/2 particle's standard quantum mechanical statistics. Furthermore, we show that the theory inherently accounts for both spin measurement and the violation of Bell's inequalities.

This study examines the secular evolution of precessing compact binaries, incorporating components such as black holes, gravastars, boson stars, and neutron stars. We analyze the secular timescales for the precession of the orbital angular momentum vector, the spin of the components, and the quadrupolar deformation of the components. Our results indicate that the spin of the components and the quadrupolar deformation of the binaries precess on timescales orders of magnitude longer than the duration of gravitational-wave signals detectable by current and upcoming ground-based interferometers. Consequently, the spin of the components and quadrupolar deformation remain effectively constant throughout the signal detection period. This finding validates the use of the Post-Newtonian approximation and the Effective One Body formalism for modeling the inspiral phase of gravitational-wave signals from precessing binaries.

YOLO (You Only Live Once) has become a leading real-time object detection framework, renowned for its exceptional speed and accuracy. This paper presents a novel variant, YOLO2 ("You Only Look 10647 Times"), which significantly enhances accuracy while preserving the original framework's speed. The proposed improvements include a refined loss function, a more robust non-maximum suppression algorithm, and a more effective training strategy.

The original Minho Quotation Collection, a manually curated and annotated corpus of Portuguese quotations, was released in 2013. It encompassed 10,000 entries drawn from diverse sources, with annotations identifying the source, author, event, and emotional sentiment. This paper details the enhancements made to the resource, expanding the total to over 20,000 quotations. The updated version includes refined annotations for event types and semantic roles, along with new categories for the medium of citation and historical period. Additionally, the resource now incorporates a thesaurus for historical era labels and a thesaurus for emotional states.

Decision trees and random forests serve as foundational tools for classification and regression in data mining. This paper introduces a novel approach to constructing decision trees leveraging formal concept analysis, utilizing the decision concept lattice structure. We present a method for generating these trees based on said lattice and provide a demonstration using a real-world dataset.

Machine learning (ML) systems are increasingly integrated into critical societal domains, including healthcare, finance, and criminal justice. While recent literature has highlighted the potential for ML to perpetuate biases, existing research has largely concentrated on data and algorithmic factors, overlooking the role of evaluation practices. This study investigates how evaluation practices influence the interpretation of bias within ML. We conducted a survey of 1,000 participants to assess their views on ML evaluation and its consequences. Our findings reveal that current evaluations frequently fail to cover diverse populations and edge cases, and that existing metrics are insufficient for detecting bias. Consequently, these evaluation practices hinder our capacity to identify and mitigate bias effectively.

Recent research has increasingly focused on continual learning scenarios involving rare classes, as these situations frequently arise in practical applications. However, existing approaches often fail to adequately handle the specific challenge of recognizing novel emerging novel subclasses alongside traditional existing rare classes. To address this, we introduce a new framework termed Continual Rare-Class Recognition (CRRC). In CRRC, a model must learn to identify both previously existing novel subclasses and the original classes, while simultaneously preventing catastrophic forgetting of prior knowledge. To tackle the imbalance inherent in rare-class data, we propose a novel metric called the Continual Rare-Class F1 Score (CRF1) to evaluate performance. Furthermore, we develop a new regularization strategy that utilizes the relationships between class centroids to facilitate learning. Experimental results across three standard benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

Ptychography is a versatile imaging technique that utilizes overlapping probe data to reconstruct a complex wavefield, which can then be analyzed to derive structural details. This approach is particularly valuable for atomic-scale investigations of materials, as it offers superior angular resolution and higher efficiency compared to traditional diffraction methods. However, when probing thick samples, multiple scattering events from atoms can invert contrast, obscuring the local atomic structure. This study demonstrates that this specific challenge can be effectively addressed by combining the phase retrieval method with the phase contrast technique. By utilizing a probe optimized for the sample's structure factor, the approach maximizes contrast while minimizing the impact of multiple scattering. The efficacy of this method was validated through simulations of a thick sample composed of a (111) oriented Al/Cu superlattice.

Stochastic thermodynamics models the behavior of small, non-equilibrated systems through Langevin dynamics, where the microscopic currents are defined as random processes. This work establishes that while these Langevin currents are gauge-dependent, the asymptotic statistical properties of the currents are gauge-independent, provided the system's steady state remains gauge-invariant. This result is proven by demonstrating that the asymptotic statistics are governed by the large deviation function, which relies on the rate function associated with path-space entropic currents—a structure that is gauge-invariant. Furthermore, we show that the asymptotic statistics for the thermodynamic currents are gauge-independent, contingent upon the system's Hamiltonian and potential being gauge-independent.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are frequently utilized to handle time-series data, yet their training is notoriously difficult due to the vanishing and exploding gradient issues. Drawing inspiration from biological systems, Reservoir Computing (RC) has emerged as a promising alternative, employing a randomly connected recurrent reservoir to transform input sequences into linearly separable representations. While recent research has primarily focused on the learning capabilities of reservoirs with fixed, randomly generated structures, this study investigates the impact of varying reservoir architectures on learning performance. By leveraging topological data analysis, we examine how complex topological characteristics of different reservoir structures influence their dynamic behavior and learning efficacy. Our findings reveal that reservoirs exhibiting specific topological traits—namely higher Betti numbers and enhanced persistence homology—demonstrate superior learning performance. Furthermore, we observed that the learning capacity of the reservoir correlates with its topological features, suggesting that the learning ability of a reservoir can be predicted by analyzing its underlying topology.

This study investigates how Efimov states influence the time-evolution of a three-bosonic system featuring pairwise interactions and a confining potential. Specifically, we examine the system's behavior when the two-body scattering length is suddenly altered from a value near a resonance producing a bound state to an infinitely large value. Our findings indicate that, under these conditions, the system's binding energy can be reduced to approximately one-third of its initial amount. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this quench process can yield binding energies as low as one-sixth of the original value, contingent upon the system's starting position relative to the resonance.

Quantum kernels offer a powerful framework for constructing quantum circuits that facilitate quantum machine learning. This work introduces a novel quantum kernel capable of being implemented using only a single qubit through the integration of single-qubit rotations and the Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference phenomenon. We demonstrate that the probability distribution generated by the HOM effect corresponds to the kernel's value, allowing for direct estimation of this value from a single qubit. Furthermore, we identify a key advantage of this single-qubit setup over traditional multi-qubit approaches: it is robust against phase errors, which are prevalent in current quantum hardware. We also illustrate the utility of this kernel by applying it to a specific quantum classification problem.

This paper introduces a new algorithm designed to calculate the Newtonian potential for planar regions with $N$ boundary points, achieving a computational complexity of $O(N\log N)$ for the discrete version. The approach relies on a new integral equation featuring a kernel that admits a multiplicative low-rank decomposition. Additionally, we present numerical experiments demonstrating the efficiency of this method.
